title: Vibe Programming
text:
About these readings
These are the session readings for the vibe programming track of GSCM 410, AI in Business Operations, at Brigham Young University. They are written for business students in any major.
In this track you direct an AI coding agent in plain English. You do not read or write code. At the start of the course you build and publish a small business app of your own, on an idea your instructor approves. Each session after that takes apart one aspect of that same app.
The readings use one example app throughout: The Dreamery, a made-up campus creamery that sells ice cream and cookies in its campus shop and online. Each reading shows a layer of the example shop, then asks you to find the same layer in your own app.

title: Build and Publish Your App — Vibe Programming, Session 0
section: The big idea: build first, understand after
text:
The big idea: build first, understand after
At the start of the course you will build a working business app and publish it on the internet. It should take perhaps an hour, in plain English, without writing a line of code. If you get stuck, the TAs and your instructor can help you finish.
Then you will spend ten more sessions finding out what you built.
That order is deliberate. Here is the main point of this reading: an AI agent can build a working app faster than you can understand it. So you build first, then take the app apart, one layer per session.
You cannot learn everything before you build anything. The fastest way to understand how software fits together is to have some of your own running, and to study that.
You will not become a programmer in this course. You will become a manager who can direct an AI agent, check its work and know when not to trust it. That skill is useful in any business job where software gets built, bought or changed.

title: Build and Publish Your App — Vibe Programming, Session 0
text:
What vibe programming is
Vibe programming means describing what you want in plain language and letting an AI write the code.
The name comes from Andrej Karpathy, a founding member of OpenAI. In February 2025 he described a new way of building software that he called “vibe coding.” You tell the AI what you want, it writes the code, and you barely look at the code at all. The phrase spread quickly. Collins Dictionary made it the word of the year for 2025.
People disagree about whether this is a good idea.

Skeptics say it produces builders who do not understand their own systems. That leads to more errors and to confusion about who is responsible when something breaks.
Supporters say it is the next step in a long trend. Each generation of programming tools has let people work further from the machine’s own language and closer to their own intent.

Both sides are partly right. This course is built on the overlap: let the agent write the code, and keep the understanding for yourself.
That is a real standard. Careless AI-built software has a name, “AI slop,” and some engineers now make a living cleaning it up. You do not want to be the reason your company hires one.
Business has seen this before. Outsourcing work does not outsource responsibility. A company that hires an outside firm to run its payroll still answers to its employees when a paycheck is wrong. You are outsourcing the typing. You still own the result.
Rule of thumb: if you cannot say what a part of your app does, you are not finished with it.

title: Build and Publish Your App — Vibe Programming, Session 0
section: A chatbot answers. An agent acts.
text:
A chatbot answers. An agent acts.
An agent is an AI model that works in a loop with tools, so it can take actions and see their results.
You have probably used a chatbot such as ChatGPT or Claude. You ask a question, and it writes an answer. The AI part is called a model: a program that takes in text and images and writes text back. Writing text is all a model can do.
An agent is a model that has been given tools. A tool is one action the model is allowed to ask for, such as “read this file,” “change this file” or “run this command.” A program around the model carries out each request and shows the model what happened. Then the model decides what to do next.
The difference matters in practice.









A chatbot
An agent




You ask for a sales dashboard
It describes one, or writes code for you to copy
It creates the files, runs the app and checks that it starts


Where it works
In a chat window
On your computer, in your project


What can go wrong
A wrong answer
A wrong action



The agent you will use is Claude Code, made by the company Anthropic. It can read the files in your project, change them and run commands on your computer.
This course uses Claude Code in the Claude desktop app, on its Code tab. You type in a message box and click buttons, as in any other app. The same agent also runs in a terminal, a typing-only window described below. If you prefer the terminal, you can use it. The readings point out the few places where it works differently.
Think of two people at a retail chain. An analyst can study last month’s sales and recommend a price cut. A store manager with access to the pricing system can make the change. The analyst is the chatbot. The manager is the agent. The difference is the access.
That last row of the table is the reason for session 1. An agent with access can do real work, and it can do real damage.
Rule of thumb: a chatbot gives you words to check. An agent gives you actions to check.

title: Build and Publish Your App — Vibe Programming, Session 0
section: The agent loop: gather context, act, check
text:
The agent loop: gather context, act, check
Every piece of work the agent does goes through three phases, and a bad result usually traces to one of them.








Phase
What the agent does
What goes wrong here




Gather context
Reads your files and your instructions
It never looked at the file that mattered


Act
Changes something
It changed the wrong thing, or changed too much


Check
Looks at the result of its action
It skipped the check, or the check could not see the problem



The loop repeats until the task is done or you stop it.
You may already know a loop like this. Quality management teaches plan, do, check, act (PDCA). You study the situation, make a change, check the result and adjust. The agent runs a version of that cycle many times a minute.
Worked example. You tell the agent, “The Delete button on my product list does not work.” A good run looks like this.

Gather context. It reads the file for the product screen and finds the code behind the Delete button.
Act. It sees that the code removes the product from the screen but never saves the change. It adds the save.
Check. It runs the app, deletes a test product, reloads the page and confirms the product is gone.

Now three bad runs, one for each phase.

It “fixes” a different button, because it never opened the product screen. That is a context failure.
It rewrites the whole screen and breaks the Add button. That is an action failure.
It announces “Fixed!” without ever reloading the page. That is a check failure.

The loop gives you a way to diagnose the agent. When a result is wrong, ask which phase failed. Each has a different fix.







What failed
What you do




Context
Point it to the right file, or tell it the rule it was missing


Action
Make the request smaller and more specific


Check
Tell it how to verify the result, or verify it yourself



Rule of thumb: when the agent gets it wrong, ask which phase failed before you ask it to try again.

title: Build and Publish Your App — Vibe Programming, Session 0
section: You are part of the loop
text:
You are part of the loop
The agent does the typing. You brief it, approve its actions, interrupt it and check its work.
Picture the agent as a fast, capable new hire with no memory, who takes you literally. That picture tells you your four jobs.

Brief it. The agent knows only what is in front of it. It does not know your business, your customers or what you meant but did not say.
Approve. Before some actions, Claude Code stops and asks your permission. Read what it is asking before you say yes. Session 1 covers how to decide what it may do without asking.
Interrupt. You can stop the agent at any moment by clicking the stop button or pressing the Esc key. If it is heading the wrong way, stop it and redirect. Do not wait for it to finish.
Check. The agent will tell you it is done. That is a claim. Open the app and see for yourself.

One part of the new-hire comparison breaks, and it is important. A new hire learns from yesterday. The agent does not, unless the lesson is written down where it will read it. Session 1 shows you where.
You will see some new things on the screen. Two words will help.

A terminal is a window where you control a computer by typing instead of clicking.
A command is one typed instruction, such as an instruction to delete a file.

You will not memorize commands. The agent types them, and the desktop app shows each one in the conversation. You only need to recognize that a command is an action, and that some actions are hard to undo. A deleted file does not go to the trash.
A shift supervisor has the same job. The supervisor does not do every task. The supervisor sets up the work, approves the first result, steps in when something looks wrong and inspects the output.
Rule of thumb: read before you approve, and look before you believe.

title: Build and Publish Your App — Vibe Programming, Session 0
section: What you will build in class
text:
What you will build in class
You will build a small business app of your own and publish it at a web address. Your instructor approves the idea first.
The approval is there to make sure your app has enough to it. It needs to be worth taking apart for the rest of the course. A useful shape is an app that keeps records of a few related kinds of things and calculates something a manager would act on.
The readings use one example app throughout: The Dreamery, “where sweet dreams come true.” It is a made-up campus creamery, a business that makes and sells ice cream, and it also bakes cookies. Customers buy pints and half-gallons of ice cream and boxes of cookies at the shop on campus. They can also order online and have them shipped. The Dreamery and all of its numbers are invented for these readings. If you are curious how a real campus creamery’s supply chain works, from the dairy to the freezer case, read the Marriott School’s article “Frozen Assets”.
In its first version the example shop has four parts.



Part
What it holds




Products
What the shop sells, with a price and the number in stock


Customers
Who buys from the shop


Orders
Who bought what, how many, when, and whether it has shipped


Sales dashboard
Numbers calculated from the order history



A dashboard is a screen that sums up records as a few numbers a manager can act on. The shop’s dashboard shows the best sellers and how many of each product sold per week. It also shows how many days of stock are left at that pace, and it flags any product that is running low. The owner uses it to decide what to reorder and what to stop carrying.
Your own app should have a part like this: something it calculates from the records it keeps. A club’s event app might calculate attendance trends. A tutoring service might calculate hours per tutor.
Each of you builds your own app. Do not reuse a team project from another course, because every student needs an app that is theirs to change and to break.
Two words describe where your app runs.

While you build, the app runs on your own computer, and only you can see it.
To publish an app is to put it on a computer that anyone can reach over the internet. The published copy is called the live app, and it has its own web address.

Once your app is published, you will open it on your phone.
You will sign up for a few services before class: one for the AI agent, one to store your project, one to store your data and one to publish the app. Your instructor will send the setup steps. Do them before class, because setup is slow and class time is short.
Rule of thumb: start small. An app that does four things correctly is worth more than one that does twelve things badly.

title: Build and Publish Your App — Vibe Programming, Session 0
text:
Why build before you understand
Building an app in about an hour will make you feel that you understand it. You will not, yet, and knowing that is the starting point of the course.
Psychologists Justin Kruger and David Dunning described a pattern in 1999 that now carries their names. People who are new to a skill often rate their own ability too high. They do not yet know enough to see what they are missing. This is called the Dunning-Kruger effect.
Vibe programming is a perfect setup for it. After about an hour you will have a working, published app. It will look finished. You will be tempted to conclude that building software is easy.
Then ask yourself a few questions.

Where is your app’s data stored, and who can read it?
If a number your app calculates is wrong, where would you look?
What stops a stranger from changing your records?
What will the app cost to run if a thousand people use it?
If the agent broke it tomorrow, how would you get yesterday’s version back?

You will not be able to answer most of them. That is expected. Each one is a session of this course.
A store visit works the same way. After an hour in the aisles, a visitor feels they understand the business. The store manager knows about the late deliveries, the theft, the slow sellers and the register that freezes on busy days. The course moves you from the visitor’s view toward the manager’s.
Engineers learn a competitor’s product by doing a teardown. They take it apart, one layer at a time, and ask why each part is there. That is the plan for the next ten sessions, applied to your own app.







Session
What you take apart




1
Directing the agent: what it can see, what it may do, how you check it


2
Architecture: the parts of an app and how they fit


3
GitHub: save points, review and the human in the loop


4
User experience: screens people can actually use


5
Testing: how you know it works


6
Databases: where the data lives


7
Logins and security: who may do what


8
Deployment: publishing, and undoing a bad publish


9
Connections: reaching other systems


10
AI in your app: models and what they cost



Each session follows the same rhythm. You find that session’s layer in your own app. You learn the idea in plain English. You direct the agent to change it. You break something and fix it. Then you discuss what it means for a business.
Rule of thumb: treat a feeling of “this is easy” as a sign that the Dunning-Kruger effect may be at work, and ask one more question.

title: Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1
section: The big idea: you are the manager
text:
The big idea: you are the manager
In session 0 an AI agent built your app while you mostly watched. This session you learn to direct it.
The readings use one example app, The Dreamery, a made-up campus creamery that sells ice cream and cookies in its campus shop and online. It has four parts:

Products: what the shop sells, with a price and the number in stock.
Customers: who buys from the shop.
Orders: who bought what, how many, when the order was placed, the date the shop promised to ship it and the date it actually shipped.
A sales dashboard: numbers calculated from the order history.

The dashboard shows three numbers for each product. Units sold per week is the average number sold each week over the last four weeks. Days of stock left is the number in stock divided by the average number sold per day. A low-stock alert flags any product with fewer than 14 days of stock left.
Your own app keeps its own records and calculates its own numbers. As you read, find the matching piece in your app.
Here is the main point of the session: you control an agent by answering three questions.

What can it see? The agent works only from the information in front of it.
What may it do? You decide which actions it takes alone and which wait for you.
How will you know it worked? The agent’s report is a claim. Your own check is the evidence.

Think of the agent as a capable new employee on the first day of work. The new hire knows how a shop works but knows nothing about your products, your rules or your priorities. You would brief that person, set a spending limit and review the first few decisions. You will do the same three things with the agent.
The rest of this reading covers one habit and then the three questions.
crumbs: 2  Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1

title: Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1
text:
Build by conversation
You get better results from a series of small requests than from one large one.
You do not need a perfect prompt. You need a conversation: ask for one small thing, look at the result, then ask for the next.
Compare two ways of asking for the same improvement to the dashboard.
One large request: “Add low-stock warnings with color coding, a ranking of products, a monthly report and a reorder suggestion.” The agent builds all of it at once. If the ranking looks wrong, you cannot tell which part caused the problem.
A conversation:

“Add a column to the dashboard showing each product’s days of stock left.” You check it.
“Show the number in red when it is below 14.” You check it.
“Sort the list so the lowest number is at the top.” You check it.

Each step is small enough to check in a minute. A mistake is caught before the next step is built on top of it.
A marketer does the same thing with a big email campaign. They send it to a small test group first and check the results before sending it to everyone. A small request is your test send.
Three habits make the conversation work:

Say what you want and why. “The owner needs to see what to reorder at a glance” helps the agent more than “add colors.”
Think out loud. If you are unsure, say so, and ask the agent for two or three options.
Write it down once it is settled. Conversation is for exploring. When you know what you want to keep, put it in writing, so the next conversation does not have to rediscover it.

Rule of thumb: if you could not check a request in a minute or two, split it.

title: Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1
text:
Question 1: What can it see?
The agent can use only what is in front of it right now.
Everything the agent can read at one moment is called its context. The context holds the tool’s own built-in instructions, your instruction file (covered below), your messages and the agent’s replies. It also holds the results of the agent’s actions, such as files it opened.
Whatever is not in the context does not exist for the agent. That includes yesterday’s conversation, a decision you made in your head and a file it never opened.
Context has two limits that surprise new users.

It is finite. In a long conversation, older material is summarized to make room. An instruction you gave early on can be lost in the summary.
It does not carry over. A conversation is one continuous exchange with the agent. Claude Code’s own screens call it a “session.” A new conversation starts without your earlier messages.

A restaurant runs on the same limit. The dinner shift knows only what the lunch shift wrote in the handover notes. Anything said out loud at noon and never written down is gone by 6 p.m.
Worked example. On Monday you tell the agent, “Leave cancelled orders out of every sales number.” It does. On Wednesday you start a new conversation and ask for a weekly sales report. The report counts cancelled orders. The agent did not disobey you. The instruction you gave on Monday did not carry over to Wednesday’s new conversation, so the agent never saw it.
Two controls help you manage context.









What you want
Desktop app
In the terminal
When to use it




See what is filling the context
Open the Context card in the session rail beside the chat (click Show session rail in the conversation’s title bar)
Type /context
When the agent seems to be forgetting


Start a new, empty conversation
Click + New in the sidebar
Type /clear
When you switch to a different task



In a new conversation, everything you said before is gone. Your instruction file still loads. That difference is the subject of the next section.

title: Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1
section: The instruction file: what the agent sees every time
text:
The instruction file: what the agent sees every time
Anything that must survive goes in a file the agent re-reads, not in a chat message.
Claude Code reads a file named CLAUDE.md at the start of every conversation. This reading calls it the instruction file. It is plain text, and it holds the things you would otherwise explain again and again.
Think of the opening checklist taped inside a restaurant’s kitchen door. It does not depend on who is on shift or what was said yesterday. Whoever starts work reads the same sheet.
Write what the agent cannot work out by reading your app: your decisions, your business rules and your limits. A good instruction file for the example shop has four parts.







Part
Example for the shop




What the app is
“The records for a small campus creamery that sells ice cream and cookies in its shop and online: products, customers, orders and a sales dashboard.”


How the business talks
“Days of stock left is the number in stock divided by average daily sales over the last 28 days. Cancelled orders never count as sales.”


What done means
“A change is not done until the app runs and I have seen the new feature work.”


What to leave alone
“Never publish the live app or change customer records without asking me first.”



You do not have to write it from a blank page. Ask the agent to draft one, or type /init, which writes a starter file by reading your project. Then edit the draft the way you would edit a new employee’s job description.
Keep the file short. Claude’s documentation suggests fewer than 200 lines. Every line takes up context in every conversation, and a long file is followed less reliably.
Keep it current as well. If you change a business rule, change the file the same day. An out-of-date instruction misleads every conversation that reads it.
Claude Code also saves some notes of its own as it works. It decides what to save, and the notes stay on one computer. Do not rely on them for a rule you care about.
Rule of thumb: if you have told the agent something twice, it belongs in the instruction file.
crumbs: 2  Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1

title: Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1
text:
Question 2: What may it do?
Before you let the agent act alone, ask how far the action reaches and whether you can undo it.
An action’s blast radius is everything it can change if it goes wrong. The farther an action reaches, the fewer ways you have to undo it.
Claude Code helps with the nearest kind of action. It saves a checkpoint, a snapshot of your files, before each message you send. To rewind is to restore your files to an earlier checkpoint. Your instructor will show you how to rewind in the desktop app. In the terminal, you type /rewind. A checkpoint covers only the edits the agent makes with its own file-editing tool. It does not cover anything else.
So every action falls into one of three groups.









Group
Example in the shop
How you undo it
So you




1. The agent edits a file in your project
Renaming the “Items” heading to “Products”; adding a days-of-stock column
Rewind
Let it run


2. The agent runs a command that deletes or moves files on your computer
Deleting the folder of old sample data
Only from a save point you made earlier (session 3)
Make a save point first


3. The action leaves your computer
Publishing the live app; changing the live customer records; sending an email
You cannot. You can only fix it afterward.
Approve it yourself



You already know this pattern from billing. A typo in a draft invoice costs nothing to fix. An invoice already emailed to a customer takes an apology and a corrected copy. A payment already sent to the wrong account may never come back.
Group 3 deserves the most care. Once the live app is published, people may have seen the wrong page. Once the live customer records are changed, the old values are gone unless someone kept a backup. Once an email is sent, it is in someone’s inbox.
In this course, your project is stored on a service called GitHub, and sending your changes there also updates your live app. Treat that step as a group 3 action. Session 3 covers GitHub and save points. Session 8 covers publishing.
Rule of thumb: ask two questions before each kind of action. How far does it reach? Can I undo it?

title: Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1
section: Modes and rules: setting the approval limit
text:
Modes and rules: setting the approval limit
A mode sets how much the agent does without asking. A rule makes it stop no matter what.

Three modes
A mode is a setting that decides which actions the agent takes without your approval. Claude Code has several. You need three this session.








Mode
What the agent does
Use it when




Plan
Reads your project, looks around and writes a plan. It does not change your files until you approve the plan.
The task is large, unclear or risky


Manual
Reads on its own. Asks you before each change or action.
You are learning, or the work is sensitive


Auto
Works without stopping to ask. A second AI model reviews each action first and blocks the ones that look risky.
The task is long, routine and easy to undo



Always check which mode you are in before you start. In the desktop app, you pick the mode from a selector under the message box. The app remembers the last mode you picked for each project, except plan mode, so a new conversation may start in auto. Do not assume the agent will ask first. In the terminal, recent versions start in auto, and pressing Shift+Tab changes the mode.
Match the mode to the blast radius. Renaming a heading across the app is a group 1 action, so auto is fine. Changing every product price in the live data is group 3. Have the agent plan it in plan mode, read the plan, and then approve the action yourself.


Advice is not enforcement
Your instruction file is advice. The agent usually follows it, but not every time. A later message in the chat can even talk it out of a written instruction.
Auto mode’s reviewer is not a guarantee either. It allows routine work, and it can treat sending your changes to GitHub as routine.
For a line that must never be crossed without you, use a permission rule. A permission rule is a setting that Claude Code checks before the agent acts, whatever the agent has decided. Two kinds matter here.

An ask rule makes the agent stop and ask you every time, even in auto mode.
A deny rule blocks the action outright, in every mode.

Company spending works the same way. A memo that says “get approval for any purchase over $5,000” is advice, and a rushed employee can ignore it. An approval limit built into the company’s purchasing system is enforcement. The system will not release the payment until a manager approves it.
You will not write permission rules yourself this session. Your instructor will show you where they are set. Your job is to know which lines need one. Publishing the live app is the first.
Rule of thumb: if a rule must hold every single time, it cannot live only in the instruction file.
crumbs: 2  Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1

title: Directing the Agent — Vibe Programming, Session 1
section: Question 3: How will you know it worked?
text:
Question 3: How will you know it worked?
A task is done when you have seen it work, not when the agent says it is done.
An agent stops when the work looks finished to it. Its report is sincere and sometimes wrong. If the only check is one the agent wrote for itself, the check can be wrong in the same way the work is wrong.
A store receives deliveries on the same principle. It does not pay because the driver’s slip says “40 boxes.” Someone counts the boxes. Treat the agent’s report like the driver’s slip.
Use three checks, in order.

Look at what changed. Ask the agent to list every file it changed and to explain each change in plain English. If it touched something you did not ask about, find out why.
Run the app and use the feature. Click through it the way a customer or the owner would.
Confirm the behavior you asked for, including the awkward cases. An edge case is an unusual situation where software tends to break.

Worked example. You ask for a “Shipped late” flag on any order that shipped after its promised ship date. The agent adds it and tests it with an order that shipped three days late. The flag appears, and the agent reports success.
You run the app. Every order that shipped on its promised date is also marked late. The cause is small. The computer stored each promised date as midnight at the start of that day. A package that left at 2 p.m. on the right day left “after” midnight, so it counted as late.
The agent’s test tried only an order that was three days late, so the test passed. The agent’s work and the agent’s test missed the same case. Your own rule caught it: an order that ships on its promised date is on time.
This is where your business knowledge beats the agent’s. You know which cases happen in a real shop:

An order that ships on the promised date itself.
An order that has not shipped yet.
A new product with no sales yet, so there is nothing to divide by.
An order that ships in two parts.

You can also check the arithmetic by hand. Suppose a flavor has 60 pints in stock and sold 140 pints in the last 28 days. That is 5 pints a day, so days of stock left must be 12. If the dashboard says anything else, the dashboard is wrong.
Two habits make checking faster:

Predict before you look. Before you read the agent’s report, write down one result that would prove the feature works. Add one edge case that might break it. Then check both.
Ask for evidence. “Show me the flag for an order shipped early, on the promised date and three days late” gets more than “does it work?”

Match the check to the risk. A changed heading or color needs only a look at what changed. Anything that calculates, saves data or changes what a customer or the owner sees needs all three checks.

title: Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2
section: The big idea: three places and the messages between them
text:
The big idea: three places and the messages between them
In session 1 you learned to direct the agent. You asked for changes to your app, and the agent decided where each piece went. It has been making those decisions since the intro session.
This session you find out what it built. Architecture is the plan of an app: its main parts and how they connect.
Here is the main point of the session: your app is three places connected by messages, and most serious problems come from something sitting in the wrong place.
You do not need to read code to use this idea. You need a map. Once you can say which place a rule or a piece of data belongs in, you can tell the agent where to put it. You can also catch the agent when it puts something in the wrong place.
crumbs: 3  Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2

title: Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2
text:
Three places
Every app is built from a browser, a server and a database, and a different party controls each one.
The browser is the program on the user’s device that shows your app, such as Chrome or Safari. Your app’s screens run inside it. The server is a computer you control that runs your app’s rules and keeps its secrets. The database is where the app stores what it must remember between visits.









Place
Also called
Who controls it
What belongs there




Browser
Frontend, client
The user
Screens, buttons, forms and quick checks that save the user time


Server
Backend
You
The rules of the business, secret keys and calls to paid services


Database
Storage
You, through its rules
Everything the app must keep: in the example shop, products, customers and orders



You will hear frontend and backend often. The frontend is what the user sees and touches. The backend is the code that runs on a computer you control.
A database stores records in tables, much like a spreadsheet. Each table has columns, and each record is one row. The example shop has a table of products, a table of customers and a table of orders. Here are two rows from its orders table.











Order number
Customer
Product
Quantity
Promised ship date
Shipped




2041
R. Alvarez
Honey Oat Swirl ice cream, pint
3
March 3
March 3


2042
J. Park
Lemon Sugar cookies, box of 6
1
March 10
(not yet)



Think of a wholesaler that takes orders on a paper form. The customer holds the order form and can write anything on it. The order desk checks each order against the company’s rules. The warehouse holds the stock. The order form is the browser, the order desk is the server and the warehouse is the database.
Worked example. Find the three places in the example shop. The sales dashboard screen is in the browser. The shop’s rule that cancelled orders never count as sales is a business rule, so it belongs on the server or in the database. The orders themselves are rows in the database. Now find the same three places in your own app.
Rule of thumb: for any piece of your app, ask who controls the place it sits in.
crumbs: 3  Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2

title: Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2
text:
Messages connect the places
The three places never share memory. They talk only by sending requests and getting responses.
A request is a message one place sends another to ask for something. A response is the reply. The browser cannot reach into the database and change a row. It has to ask.
An API is the list of requests a place agrees to answer. Your server has one, and your browser uses it. Outside services have them too. Session 9 covers APIs in detail.
Departments in a company work the same way. Sales does not walk into the warehouse and take stock off the shelf. It sends an order, and the warehouse sends back a confirmation. Every handoff is a document and a reply.
Worked example. The shop owner ships order 2042 from the table above. Follow the hops.

The owner types today’s date in the ship date box and clicks Mark shipped.
The browser runs a quick check: the box is not empty.
The browser sends a request to the server: “Mark order 2042 shipped, today’s date.”
The server checks the request again. Does order 2042 exist? Is it still open?
The server asks the database to update the row for order 2042.
The database saves the ship date, and replies that it is done.
The server sends a response to the browser: “Saved.”
The browser shows order 2042 as Shipped.

Notice that the request is checked twice, once in the browser and once on the server. The next section explains why.
In some apps the browser sends requests straight to the database for ordinary data, with no server in between. The services this course uses allow that. When it happens, the database’s own rules are the only check. Ask the agent which way your app works.

Use the trace to find a problem
The trace is also your best tool when something looks wrong.
The numbers on the shop’s dashboard are not typed in. They are calculated from the order rows each time. So a wrong number has three possible causes, one per place:

The stored data is wrong. A quantity was saved incorrectly in the database.
The rule is wrong. The calculation counts the wrong orders, such as cancelled ones.
The display is wrong. The right number arrives, and the screen shows it badly.

Suppose Honey Oat Swirl pints show 30 units sold per week, and you counted 24 by hand. Do not ask the agent to “fix the dashboard.” Ask where the number is calculated, and ask to see the rows it used. Then you know which place holds the problem.
Rule of thumb: never correct a calculated number on the screen. Find the place that produced it.
crumbs: 3  Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2

title: Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2
text:
The trust line
The user controls the browser, so a check that runs only in the browser can be skipped.
Every piece of your app that runs in the browser is first sent to the user’s device. Browsers include a panel called developer tools. It shows a page’s code, its stored data and every request the page sends. Anyone can open it. With it, a user can read what was sent to the browser, change it, and send requests by hand.
Two consequences follow.

A browser check is a courtesy. It gives honest users fast feedback. It does not stop anyone who wants to get around it.
Anything sent to the browser is public. That includes any secret placed there by mistake.

So picture a line between the browser and everything else. On the user’s side, nothing is guaranteed. Checks that matter must run again on your side of the line, on the server or in the database.
A wholesaler already works this way. A customer can write any price on an order form. You do not bill from the customer’s number. The order desk prices the order from your own price list.
Worked example. In the example shop, an order that has shipped cannot be cancelled. The agent enforces this by turning the Cancel button grey once an order ships. That is the only check. A user opens developer tools, turns the button back on and cancels order 2041, which shipped on March 3. The three pints no longer count as sold, so the dashboard’s sales numbers are wrong. Worse, a refund may follow for ice cream the customer already has.
The fix is to enforce the rule where the data lives. The server, or a rule in the database, refuses to cancel a shipped order. Keep the grey button as well. It tells honest users what they can do.
Watch for the same mistake with access. Hiding a button or a link from some users does not stop them. A user who knows the web address can still send the request. Access is enforced only when the server or the database refuses. Session 7 covers logins and access.
Rule of thumb: if a rule protects money, data or a reported number, it must be enforced on the server or in the database.
crumbs: 3  Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2

title: Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2
text:
Secrets stay on the server
A secret key is safe on the server and public the moment it reaches the browser.
Many outside services charge for use. To use one, your app sends an API key with each request. An API key is a secret string the service gives your account. It says whose account is calling, and that account gets the bill.
Your app will need one in session 10, when it calls an AI model. It may need others to send email or to reach your database with full access.
Now apply the trust line. If a key is in the browser, any user can read it with developer tools. That user can then run up your bill or read all your data. So the rule is simple. Anything that needs a secret key goes through your server. The browser asks the server, the server calls the paid service with the key, and the server passes back only the result.
A company handles its bank details the same way. The purchasing team can request a payment. Only the finance office holds the account credentials, and it makes the payment itself.
Your project keeps its secret keys in a small settings file, commonly named .env.local. That file stays on your computer and on the server. It must never be sent to GitHub, because a secret placed in a public project is published. Session 3 explains how files are kept out of GitHub.
If a secret key ever does reach the browser or a public project, treat it as public. Replace it with a new one at once, then move the work that needed it to the server.
Rule of thumb: if a user could read it in the browser, it is not a secret.

section: Who runs each place: the stack
text:
Who runs each place: the stack
You control the server and the database, but other companies own the computers they run on.
A stack is the set of technologies an app is built from. Yours has a name for each part.








Part of the app
What can do the job in this course
What it is




Screens and server code
Next.js
A toolkit for writing both the browser screens and the server code in one project


Hosting
Vercel (or GitHub Pages, for an app with no server code)
The company whose computers run your app and serve it at a web address


Database
Supabase
A company that runs your database for you, and can also handle sign-in


Project storage
GitHub
Where your project’s files and their history are kept (session 3)



Hosting means running an app on computers that other people can reach over the internet.
These are the services the readings use as examples. They are not the only choices, and some students will use others that do the same job. Whatever your app uses, you should be able to name the service for each row.
This is the same choice a business makes about space. A small shop rarely builds its own building. It rents the space and keeps control of the business inside it. You rent the computers and keep control of the app.
There are two copies of your app. While you build, a copy runs on your own computer at an address beginning with localhost. That name always means “this computer,” and nothing there leaves your machine. The live copy runs on the hosting company’s computers, where anyone with the address can reach it. In session 1 terms, changes to the computer copy are in groups 1 and 2. Changes to the live copy are in group 3.
Other stacks exist, and none is the only reasonable choice. The advice for a first product is to pick a well-known, well-documented one. Its problems are already known and written about. An agent also writes better code for a popular stack, because it has seen far more examples.

You speak English; the agent writes code
You direct the agent in plain English, but it does not build your app in English. It writes code: instructions in a programming language, a precise written language that computers can follow. Each place in your app has its usual languages.








Where it runs
Common languages
What they do




Browser (frontend)
HTML, CSS, JavaScript
HTML lays out what is on a screen, CSS sets how it looks, and JavaScript makes it respond to clicks


Server (backend)
TypeScript, JavaScript, Python, Java, Rust and others
Run the business rules and talk to the database


Both
TypeScript
JavaScript with extra checks added, so mistakes are caught before the app runs



Browsers understand only HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so every app’s screens end up in those three. The server side has more choice. The projects in this course use TypeScript for both.
These languages are standards for the same reason accountants share one set of accounting rules. Millions of people already know them. They are well documented, and free building blocks exist for almost any task. An AI agent has also learned from huge amounts of code written in them, so it writes them well.
You will not need to write or read any of these languages. Knowing their names helps you read the map later in this reading and follow what the agent tells you.
Rule of thumb: when something breaks, first ask which service runs the place where it broke.

title: Architecture: The Pieces and How They Fit — Vibe Programming, Session 2
section: Read the map, then direct by place
text:
Read the map, then direct by place
A file’s name and folder tell you where it runs. A request that names each place gets each piece put in the right place.

Reading the map
Your project is a set of files. You do not need to read the code inside them, and no one expects you to understand it. You are welcome to look. Just do not change a file by hand unless you know what you are doing; ask the agent to make the change instead. You can read the map without reading the code, because the stack follows naming rules.
A library works this way. A book’s call number tells you the section and the shelf before you open the book. A file’s folder and name do the same job.








Example file or folder
What it holds
Where it runs




app/products/page.tsx
One screen. The folder path is its web address: /products
Server or browser. Ask the agent.


app/api/orders/route.ts
The server code that answers requests about orders
Server only


components/
Screen pieces used on more than one screen
Often the browser


supabase/migrations/
Each change made to the database’s tables
Database


.env.local
Secret keys and settings
Server. Never sent to GitHub.


CLAUDE.md
Your instruction file from session 1
Read by the agent. Not part of the running app.



Your file names may differ a little. The pattern will not. The ending of a file’s name tells you its language: .tsx and .ts files are TypeScript, and .md files are plain text.
To see the map yourself in the desktop app, open the Files pane: click its button, or choose it from the ⋮ menu beside the pane buttons. It shows your project’s files, and you can click one to look inside. You can also ask the agent to draw the map for you: “List every file in this project and label it browser, server, database or tools only. Explain how you decided.” Then check two of its labels against the table. That is session 1’s third question applied to a map.


Directing by place
Once you can see the places, name them in your requests. Compare two requests for the same feature.
Vague: “Let the owner cancel an order.”
By place:

Browser: add a Cancel button on each order that has not shipped, with a box for a reason. Show a message if the cancel fails.
Server: refuse to cancel an order that has already shipped. Require a reason.
Database: store the status Cancelled, the reason and the date. Never delete the row.
Dashboard: leave cancelled orders out of every sales number.

The second request says where each rule is enforced. The browser part is there for convenience. The enforcing rules sit where the user cannot reach them.
A restaurant ticket does the same thing in a kitchen. It tells the grill, the fryer and the salad station what each one makes. Nobody has to guess who does what.
When you are unsure where something belongs, ask before the agent builds. Use plan mode from session 1: “Before changing anything, explain what will run in the browser, what will run on the server, what the database will store, and where each rule is enforced.”
Rule of thumb: a request is ready when it says what happens in each place and where each rule is enforced.

title: GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3
section: The big idea: a way back and a gate
text:
The big idea: a way back and a gate
In session 1 you sorted the agent’s actions into three groups. Group 2 was the uncomfortable one. When the agent runs a command that deletes or moves files, rewinding to a checkpoint cannot help. You needed a save point, and the reading promised one in session 3.
In session 2 you learned that your project is a set of files. You also learned that the live copy of your app runs on a hosting company’s computers.
This session connects the two. The agent can change your project many times a day. If you cannot safely change your app, you no longer control it.
Here is the main point of the session: version control gives you a way back to any earlier state of your project, and a gate every change passes before users see it.
Version control is a system that records every change to a set of files. The one your project uses is called Git. GitHub is a website that stores a copy of your project and its history online, for backup, sharing and review.
You will rarely type a Git command. The agent does that when you ask in plain English. Your job is to know what each step means, and to be the person at the gate.
crumbs: 4  GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3

title: GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3
text:
Commits: your save points
A commit is a saved snapshot of your whole project, with a message that says what changed.
When you ask the agent to save a save point, it makes a commit. The commit records every file in the project as it is at that moment. Git keeps every commit, in order, and you can return to any of them.
This is the safety net for session 1’s group 2. If the agent deletes the wrong folder, Git can bring back every file as it was in your last commit. A file you never committed is gone.
A manufacturer controls its drawings the same way. Each released version of a drawing gets a revision letter and a change note. Anyone can pull revision B and see exactly what the part looked like then. A commit is a revision of your whole project, and its message is the change note.
The message matters as much as the snapshot. Compare two histories of the same afternoon.



Useful history
Useless history




Add days-of-stock column to sales dashboard
updates


Show days of stock in red below 14
more changes


Leave cancelled orders out of sales numbers
fix



In the first history you can find the exact point you want to return to. In the second you cannot.
Worked example. You plan to have the agent delete the folder of old sample data. First you say, “Save a save point called ‘Before removing old sample data.’” The agent deletes the folder, and one file the product screen needed goes with it. You say, “Bring back the project as it was at the last save point.” The file returns. Without the commit, it would be gone.
Two habits make commits useful:

Commit small. One finished piece of work per commit. A commit that mixes five changes is hard to undo without losing four good ones.
Commit before risk. Make a save point before any group 2 action.

Rule of thumb: if you would be upset to lose it, commit it.
crumbs: 4  GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3

title: GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3
section: Two copies: your computer and GitHub
text:
Two copies: your computer and GitHub
A commit stays on your computer until you push it. A push leaves your computer.
Your project lives in two places. One copy, with its full history, is on your computer. The other is on GitHub.

A push copies your new commits from your computer to GitHub.
A pull copies new commits from GitHub to your computer.

Now apply session 1’s blast radius. A commit is local. Nobody else sees it, and it can be undone, so the agent can commit freely. A push is different. It reaches GitHub, and depending on where it lands, it can update your live app. A push is a group 3 action.
That gives you a standing rule for your instruction file: commit freely, and push only when I say so.
An advertising team works the same way. A designer can revise an ad on their own computer all day. Nothing reaches customers until the ad is sent to the printer. A commit is a saved revision. A push is sending it out.

What must never be pushed
Session 2 introduced .env.local, the file that holds your secret keys. It must never reach GitHub, because a secret in a public project is published.
Git handles this with a file named .gitignore. It is a list of files that Git must not track. Files on that list are never committed, so they are never pushed. Your project’s .gitignore should include your secrets file.
You can check in one sentence: “Which files in this project are ignored by Git, and why is each one ignored?” If the secrets file is not on the list, have the agent fix that before the next commit.
Rule of thumb: a commit is a note to yourself. A push is a message to the world.
crumbs: 4  GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3

title: GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3
section: Branches: a side line for each change
text:
Branches: a side line for each change
A branch lets you build and test a change without touching the version your users see.
Your project has one official line of commits, named main. Your live app is built from main. Every new commit that reaches main on GitHub is published to the live app.
A branch is a separate line of commits that starts from main and does not change it. You can commit to a branch all afternoon. main and the live app stay exactly as they were.
A restaurant does this with a test kitchen. A new dish is tried in the back while the regular menu keeps serving customers. If the trial fails, diners never knew. If it works, the dish goes on the menu.
Worked example. In the example shop, the owner wants to keep notes on each customer. You say, “Start a new branch called customer-notes and do this work there.” The agent adds a notes box to the customer screen and saves two commits on the branch. Anyone using the live app sees no change. The work is real, saved and out of the way.
Give each branch one task and a name that says what the task is. customer-notes tells you what is on it. test2 does not.
Rule of thumb: one task, one branch.
crumbs: 4  GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3

title: GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3
text:
The pull request: the gate
A pull request holds a change at the gate while it is checked, previewed and reviewed. Nothing reaches the live app until someone merges it.
A pull request is a page on GitHub that asks to add one branch’s commits to main. Adding them is called a merge. While the pull request is open, three things happen.

Checks run. GitHub runs a set of automated checks on the change and marks the pull request with a green check or a red X. Session 5 covers what the checks test.
A preview is built. The hosting company builds a working copy of the app with this change, at its own web address. This is the preview. It is separate from the live app.
Someone reviews. A person reads what changed, clicks through the preview, and then approves or sends the work back.

Here is one change from start to finish.








Step
What happens
Has the live app changed?




1. Branch
The agent creates the branch customer-notes.
No


2. Commit
The agent builds the feature and commits it to the branch.
No


3. Push and open
The agent pushes the branch to GitHub and opens a pull request.
No


4. Checks and preview
The checks run, and a preview is built.
No


5. Review
You read the changes and try the preview.
No


6. Merge
You merge the pull request. The commits join main.
About to


7. Publish
The hosting company publishes the new main to the live app.
Yes



A company handles a new policy the same way. The change is written up, reviewed by the people it affects and checked by legal. Only after sign-off is it announced to employees.

What to read in a review
The page for a pull request shows the diff: every line added, removed or changed, compared with main. You do not read code, but you can still review a diff in three ways.

Read the list of changed files. Session 2 taught you to read file names. Did the agent change a file your request had nothing to do with?
Ask a fresh conversation to review it. Start a new conversation with the agent. Ask it to explain the diff in plain English and to flag anything outside the request. A fresh conversation catches more than the one that wrote the change.
Try the preview. Use the feature the way a customer or the owner would, with session 1’s edge cases.

Worked example. You open the pull request for customer-notes. The preview looks right. Notes save and reappear. Then you read the list of changed files. One of them is the server file that handles cancelling orders. Your request had nothing to do with cancelling.
You ask a fresh conversation to explain. It reports that the agent removed the server check that refuses to cancel a shipped order. The agent had hit an error along the way and removed the check to make the error go away.
Remember session 2. That server check is what stops a shipped order from being cancelled. The grey Cancel button is still there, so the preview looks perfect. The problem is invisible in the running app and plain in the diff.
You send the work back. The agent restores the check in a new commit, the pull request updates, and only then do you merge. Without the pull request, the missing check would have gone straight to the live app.


You are the human in the loop
Three facts about the gate are worth knowing.

A red X does not lock the gate. Unless the project is set up to require passing checks, GitHub still lets you merge. Look before you click.
You cannot approve your own pull request on GitHub. When you work alone, the review is you reading the changes and the preview before you merge.
The preview may share the live database. A preview is a separate copy of the app. It may still read and write the same data as the live app. Session 8 covers how to give it data of its own.

Merging is a group 3 action. It is the moment a change leaves your control. The agent should never merge on its own.
Rule of thumb: the preview shows you what the change does. The diff shows you what else it did.
crumbs: 4  GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3

title: GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3
section: Keep changes small and merge them often
text:
Keep changes small and merge them often
A small change merged within a day or two is easier to review and undo, and less likely to collide with other work.
A branch should be short-lived. Finish the task, merge it within a day or two and delete the branch. Then start the next branch from the newest main.
The opposite is a long-lived branch, kept open for a week or more until a big feature is finished. Two things go wrong.
First, the branch drifts. main keeps changing while the branch is open. When the branch finally comes back, Git has to combine both sets of changes. Where both sides changed the same lines, Git stops with a merge conflict. Someone has to decide by hand which version is right.
Second, the diff becomes too large to review. An agent can write a thousand changed lines in a few minutes. The removed check in the last example is easy to spot in a list of three changed files. It is easy to miss in a list of sixty.
Lean manufacturing makes the same point with batch sizes. A defect in a batch of ten is found the same day, and ten units are affected. A defect in a batch of ten thousand is found weeks later.
Worked example. The shop owner wants a reorder suggestion on the dashboard, plus a monthly sales report, plus customer notes. As one branch, that is a week of work and one enormous review. As three branches, each is a day of work and a short review. If the report turns out wrong, you undo the report and keep the other two.
Is a branch always required? Committing straight to main skips the gate. There is no preview, and nobody reads the diff before users see the change. It is reasonable only for a small change, such as a typo, when you work alone and have checked the app first. In this course, use a branch and a pull request for every change.
Rule of thumb: if a change takes more than a day or two, split it.
crumbs: 4  GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3

title: GitHub: Save Points, Review and the Human in the Loop — Vibe Programming, Session 3
section: Going back, and what going back cannot undo
text:
Going back, and what going back cannot undo
You can undo a change to your project’s files. You cannot undo what the change already did to your data.
Version control gives you two ways back.








Situation
What you ask for
What happens




The work is not pushed yet
“Bring the project back to the last save point.”
Your files return to that commit.


A bad change was already merged
“Revert that commit.”
The agent makes a new commit that undoes the old one. Merging it publishes the undo.



A revert does not erase history. The bad commit and the commit that undoes it both stay in the record. That is deliberate. You can always see what happened.
Small merges make this easy. If the last merge changed one thing, you know which commit to revert.
Now the limit. Commits record your project’s files. They do not record the rows in your database. Suppose a bad change went live for an hour and marked forty orders as shipped. Reverting the change restores the old code. The forty rows stay wrong.
A publisher knows this problem. It can fix a misprint for the next printing in a minute. The copies already sold still carry the misprint.
So match your caution to what the change touches. A change to a screen can be reverted cleanly. A change that alters or deletes stored data deserves a backup first, and a careful review at the gate. Session 6 covers the database. Session 8 covers undoing a bad publish quickly.
Rule of thumb: code has an undo. Data needs a backup.

Adapted and simplified from three of Scott Murff’s chapters, Interface and Flow, Design Fundamentals and Testing the Design, in his textbook Intro to Product Management. The ideas are his. The wording and the business examples were written for these readings.
Reading time: about 20 minutes. Class opens with a short quiz on this reading.
By the end of this session you can:

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
text:
Map the flow of a task before you ask for any screen.
Check whether a screen has one clear primary action.
Name the four states a screen has besides the one where everything goes right.
Rewrite a vague label or message, and give the agent a precise design instruction.
Run a short usability test by watching people instead of asking them.
crumbs: 5  User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
section: The big idea: the agent will not tell you the app is confusing
text:
The big idea: the agent will not tell you the app is confusing
Your app works. In session 2 you learned where its parts live. In session 3 you learned to change it safely. This session you ask a different question: can a person who has never seen it get their work done?
User experience, or UX, is everything a person goes through while using a product to reach a goal.
An agent is good at making a screen look polished. Colors, fonts and spacing are its strongest skill. But looks are the smallest part of the job. Underneath are harder questions. What steps does the task take? What is on each screen, and what is it called? What does the user think is happening?
An agent answers those questions silently, with whatever it guessed. It will build a working app that nobody can figure out, and it will not tell you.
Here is the main point of the session: every screen should make the next step obvious, and most of what users experience happens when things do not go perfectly. Judging that is your job.
crumbs: 5  User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
text:
Flows before screens
Map the steps of the task first, then ask for the screens those steps need.
A flow is the sequence of steps a user takes to finish one task. Ask an agent for “a shipping screen” and you will get one, with whatever steps it guessed. The flow is where you decide what the app asks of a person.
A flow has five parts.








Part
What it is
The question it answers




Goal
The one job the user came to do
What does “done” look like?


Entry point
Where the flow starts
How do they arrive?


Steps
Each screen or action, in order
What is the one thing they do here?


Decisions
Points where the path branches
What choice is made, and where does each choice lead?


Exits
Every way the flow can end
Where do they end up, and can they get back?



Event planners do this already. They map a guest’s path from the door to the seat before they order the decorations. A beautiful room that guests cannot find their way through is still wrong.
Worked example. Here is the flow for shipping an order in the example shop.
GOAL: Record that order 2042 shipped.

ENTRY  The list of orders waiting to ship
 1.  Open order 2042
 2.  Click "Ship"
 3.  Enter the quantity packed and the tracking number
 4.  Confirm
       DECISION: did everything on the order ship?
         all of it  -> EXIT: order is closed, stock goes down, and the dashboard updates
         part of it -> EXIT: order stays open, showing what is still owed
 CANCEL at any step before Confirm -> nothing is saved
Writing it out raises questions that a picture of a screen hides. What happens when the customer ordered three pints and only two are in the freezer? What if a package is lost? Can a shipped order be corrected? Each of these is a business decision. If you do not make it, the agent makes it for you.
Count the steps and the decisions. Each one is a place where a busy user can stop or go wrong. Remove steps the user does not care about, and make sure every exit leads somewhere useful.
Rule of thumb: write the flow before you ask for the screen, and paste the flow into your request.
crumbs: 5  User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
text:
One primary action per screen
Each screen should have one action that stands out, so the user knows what to do without reading everything.
People do not read a screen from top to bottom. They scan it, and their eyes go to whatever stands out. If everything stands out equally, nothing does. The user must read every label to find the next step.
A designer ranks the items on a screen with five tools: size, boldness, color, the empty space around an item, and position. The action most users came for gets the strongest treatment. Everything else is made quieter on purpose.
A grocery store ranks its products the same way. The best sellers sit at eye level. Slower items go on the bottom shelf. Nothing is thrown away. It is ranked.
Worked example. The agent builds the shop’s order screen with five buttons in a row, all the same blue: Ship, Edit, Cancel order, Print packing slip and Email customer. The owner pauses and reads all five. Worse, Cancel order sits right next to Ship, the same size and color.
The fix removes nothing. Ship becomes the one large, filled button. Edit becomes a plain outlined button. Print packing slip and Email customer become small text links. Cancel order moves away from Ship and asks for confirmation.
You can test any screen in ten seconds with the squint test. Squint at the screen, or blur a screenshot, until you cannot read the words. Whatever still stands out is what users will see first. If that is not the primary action, the ranking is wrong.
Rule of thumb: before you squint, write down the one action you want. Then see whether the screen agrees.
crumbs: 5  User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
text:
Off the happy path
A screen has more states than the one you demonstrated, and the others are where users get stuck.
The happy path is the run through the app where everything goes right. The data exists, the connection is fast and the input is valid. An agent builds the happy path first, because that is what your request described.
Real users spend a lot of time elsewhere. Every screen has four more states, and each needs to be designed on purpose.








State
When it happens
What a good one does




Empty
First use, or nothing to show yet
Explains what will appear here and offers one action to start


Loading
The app is waiting for data
Shows that something is coming


Error
Something failed
Says what happened in plain words, keeps what the user typed and offers a next step


Partial
Some data loaded and some did not
Shows what exists and marks what is missing



Each state should answer two questions: what is true right now, and what can I do next?
A customer service team is built around the same fact. The script for a happy customer is one line. Most of the training covers the exceptions: late packages, wrong items, refunds and upset callers.
Worked example. Look at the shop’s dashboard for a product added yesterday. It has no sales yet. An agent-built app often shows a blank area here, or “Days of stock left: 0.” Zero says the product is about to run out, which is false. Nobody has bought it yet. A good empty state says, “No sales yet. Days of stock left appears after the first order.”

Buttons that change data
One case deserves its own rule. Suppose the owner clicks Ship and nothing on the screen changes for two seconds. The owner assumes the click missed and clicks again. The action runs twice. The stock count drops twice, and the dashboard now shows less stock than the shelf holds.
Every button that saves, sends or deletes needs two kinds of feedback. It should change the moment it is pressed. Then it should stay disabled, showing that it is working, until the action finishes.
Rule of thumb: for each main screen, ask the agent to show you all four states with sample data, and look at each one.
crumbs: 5  User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
text:
Words are interface
Labels, buttons and messages are the instructions for using your app, and specific words beat clever ones.
Every word a user has to puzzle over slows them down. Two rules cover most cases.

A button says what happens when you press it. Use a verb and an object. “Ship 3 pints” tells the user more than “Submit.”
Use the user’s words, not the database’s. The owner says “days of stock left.” The owner does not say “dsl_calc” or “record.”

A recipe runs on the same discipline. It says “Add 2 cups of flour.” It does not say “Process ingredients.” Vague words in a recipe become ruined cakes.
Error messages matter most. A good one says what happened, why, and what to do next. It does not blame the user, and it does not throw away what they typed.
Worked example. Three rewrites for the example shop.








Before
After
Why it is better




Button: Submit
Ship 3 pints
Says what will happen


“Something went wrong.”
“This order has already shipped, so it cannot be shipped again. Open the order to see what was sent.”
Says what happened, why, and what to do


A blank list
“No orders waiting to ship. New orders appear here when customers place them.”
Explains the emptiness and offers the next step



Rule of thumb: copy out every button label in your app. Circle each one that does not say what happens.
crumbs: 5  User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
text:
Sketch first, then direct precisely
Ask for a rough sketch before a polished screen, and tell the agent exactly what to change and why.

Sketch first
Designers describe their drafts by fidelity: how closely a draft matches the finished product. A rough sketch is low fidelity. A mockup, a styled picture of a finished screen, is high fidelity.
High fidelity used to be expensive, so people sketched first to save work. An agent removed the cost. It can produce a polished screen in a minute. That creates a new risk. People react to what they are shown. Show someone a rough sketch, and they comment on whether the steps make sense. Show them a polished screen, and they comment on the colors.
So name your question first, then ask for the cheapest draft that answers it.







Your question
Ask the agent for




Are these the right steps and screens?
A rough text sketch of each screen, with no code written


What is on each screen, and what is it called?
A plain gray-box layout with the real labels


Does it look right and read clearly?
A styled mockup


Can a person finish the task without help?
A working version to click through



Architects work this way. They show a client a rough floor plan before any drawing of finished rooms. Moving a wall on paper costs nothing. Moving a real one is expensive, and by then everyone argues about the paint.


Direct precisely
“Make it look better” gives the agent no problem to fix. It will change things at random. A useful design instruction has five parts.







Part
Example




Where
“On the order screen, the row of buttons”


What is wrong
“Five equal buttons, so the owner reads all of them before acting”


Why
“One primary action per screen”


What to change
“Make Ship the only filled button. Outline Edit. Turn Print packing slip and Email customer into text links.”


Reference
A screenshot of your screen, or of an app that does it well



Claude Code accepts images, so a screenshot is often the best reference you can give.


Decide once
The agent has no memory between conversations. Left alone, it will style each new screen from scratch, and after ten conversations you will have five styles of button. The fix is the one from session 1. Put your design decisions in your instruction file:

One filled button per screen. Everything else is outlined or a text link.
Every list has an empty state with one sentence and one action.
Every button that saves or deletes shows that it is working and cannot be clicked twice.
Deleting or cancelling asks for confirmation.

Rule of thumb: when you catch yourself fixing the same design problem twice, write the rule down.
crumbs: 5  User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4

title: User Experience: Screens People Can Actually Use — Vibe Programming, Session 4
text:
Watch, do not ask
You find out whether an app is usable by watching people try to use it, not by asking what they think.
You built this app. You know where every button is. A new user does not. This is called the curse of knowledge: once you know something, it is almost impossible to imagine not knowing it. The agent has the same problem. It knows what every element was meant to do, so it cannot stand in for a first-time user.
A usability test means watching a real user try a real task while you stay quiet and take notes. It is not a demonstration, and it is not a survey.
Lean calls this going to the gemba, the place where the work happens. A manager who wants to know how a process really runs does not read the procedure or ask in a meeting. The manager goes to the floor and watches.
Four rules make a test work.

Use about five people. The first tester shows you a lot. Later testers mostly repeat the same problems. So test five, fix the worst problem and test again with new people.
Give a goal, not instructions. Say, “A customer ordered three pints of Honey Oat Swirl, but only two are in the freezer. Ship what you can.” Do not say, “Click Ship.”
Stay silent. Do not help, explain or defend. Let them struggle. Ask them to think out loud.
Record what they did before what they said. A tester who says “this is easy” after three wrong clicks has told you two things. The clicks are the reliable one.

Worked example. You watch five classmates try the Honey Oat Swirl task. Four of them type 2, click Ship and then look for a way to say that one pint is still owed. The app has closed the order. Nobody complained. All four said the app was “pretty clear.” You would never have found the problem by asking.
Afterward, rank what you saw by how badly it blocks the task. A problem that stops users from finishing comes first. A dated-looking icon comes last. Fix the top one or two, then test again, because a fix can fail or create a new problem.
Classmates are good practice, and they will find where a newcomer gets confused. They are not the people who pack orders every day. Before you trust a result, test with people who do the real job.
Rule of thumb: never ask “do you like it?” Ask them to do something, and watch.
