title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
text:
Learning objectives
Adapted and simplified from two of Scott Murff’s chapters, Tests and Tech Debt and The Browser, Developer Tools, and Claude in Chrome, in his textbook Intro to Product Management. The ideas are his. The wording and the business examples were written for these readings.
Reading time: about 20 minutes. Class opens with a short quiz on this reading.
By the end of this session you can:
crumbs: 6  Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
text:
Explain what an automated test is and read a list of test names as a statement of what is protected.
Tell apart the three sizes of test, and explain what a passing result does not tell you.
Direct the agent to test what matters, and spot a test that was changed to pass.
Explain why you run an AI code review before you send changes to GitHub.
Gather your own evidence with the reload test, the browser’s developer tools and the app’s logs.
crumbs: 6  Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
section: The big idea: every change can break something that used to work
text:
The big idea: every change can break something that used to work
Since session 1 you have checked the agent’s work by hand. You look at what changed, run the app and try the awkward cases. That works for the feature you just asked for.
It does not cover everything else. The example shop now has a dashboard, shipping, cancelling and customer notes, and your own app has grown the same way. The agent changes it many times a day, and any change can break something that used to work. A problem like that is called a regression. You cannot click through the whole app after every change.
Here is the main point of the session: an automated test checks one behavior in seconds, every time the app changes. A passing test proves only what someone thought to check.
You will not write tests. The agent writes them. Your job is to decide what must be tested and to read what the tests claim. You also need to know what a green check mark is worth.
crumbs: 6  Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
text:
What a test is
A test is a short program that runs part of your app with a chosen input and compares the result with the expected answer.
Every test has the same three steps.

Choose an input.
Run the app’s code on it.
State the answer it must give.

If the result matches the expected answer, the test passes. If not, it fails, and the report shows both values so you can see what changed. All the tests in a project together are called the test suite. People say the suite is “green” when every test passes and “red” when any test fails.
A machine shop uses a go/no-go gauge the same way. The gauge is made to a known size. A part either fits it or does not. Nobody has to measure and judge each time.
Worked example. In session 1, the example shop marked an order as shipped late when it shipped on its promised date. Here is a test for that rule, in plain words.







Step
For the on-time rule




Choose an input
An order promised for March 10 and shipped on March 10


Run the code
Ask the app whether this order shipped on time


State the answer
It must say “on time”



Each test has a name, and the name is a sentence saying what the app must do. You cannot read the code inside a test. You can read the names, and a list of names reads like a specification:

An order shipped on its promised date is on time.
An order shipped one day late is late.
A cancelled order is left out of every sales number.
A shipped order cannot be cancelled.
A product with no sales shows no days of stock left.

That list tells you what is protected. It also tells you what is not. If “an order shipped in two parts” is missing from the list, nothing is checking it.
Rule of thumb: ask the agent for the list of test names, and read it for what is missing.
crumbs: 6  Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
text:
Three sizes of test
Tests differ in how much of the real app each one runs. The more it runs, the slower it is and the more kinds of failure it can find.
Session 2 gave you three places: browser, server and database. The three sizes of test line up with them.










Size
What it runs
Example in your app
What it would catch
Speed




Unit test
One rule, alone. No browser, no server, no database.
The on-time rule, given two dates
A wrong rule, such as “before” where it should say “on or before”
Thousandths of a second


Integration test
Several real pieces together, such as the server and a database
Shipping order 2042, then reading the database to see what was saved
A save that fails, or saves the wrong values
Slower


End-to-end test
The whole app, through a real browser, clicking as a user would
Open the app, ship an order and check that the dashboard changes
A step a user cannot finish, such as a button that does nothing
Seconds each



A restaurant checks food at the same three levels. The cook tastes the sauce on its own. The chef checks each plate as it is put together. Then a manager eats the whole meal the way a customer would. Each level catches problems the level below cannot see.
The usual advice is to have many unit tests, fewer integration tests and only a few end-to-end tests. The large ones are slow, and they fail for more reasons.
Two details matter to you as a manager.

Tests need their own database. Integration and end-to-end tests create and delete rows. They must run against a separate test database, never the live one.
Red in the middle is normal. The agent runs the suite after its own edits, reads the failures and fixes them. What matters is the last run before it says it is done.


The checks on a pull request
In session 3, a pull request showed a green check or a red X. Now you know what ran. The usual set has four checks.







Check
What it does




Tests
Runs the test suite


Type check
Reads the code to confirm each value is the kind of data the code expects


Lint
Reads the code and flags likely mistakes


Build
Makes the same finished version the hosting company would make



Tests run your code. The type check and the lint only read it, so they are fast and catch different mistakes. The build is the last gate. If it fails here, publishing would fail too.
Rule of thumb: a rule gets a unit test. A path that users depend on gets one end-to-end test.
crumbs: 6  Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
section: What a passing result does not tell you
text:
What a passing result does not tell you
A green suite means that none of the checks someone wrote failed. It says nothing about what nobody checked.
Four limits are worth knowing.

Untested behavior is unchecked. If no test covers partial shipments, the suite can be fully green while partial shipments are broken.
The tests share the author’s understanding. If the agent misunderstood your rule, it writes code and tests with the same mistake, and they agree with each other. You saw this in session 1.
Tests do not tell you whether the feature is the right one, or whether people can use it. That takes the usability testing from session 4.
A test can be changed to pass. This is the one to watch.

A health inspection has the same limits. “Passed inspection” means the restaurant passed the items on the checklist. Anything not on the checklist was never looked at. And there are two ways to pass a failing item: fix the kitchen, or loosen the checklist.
Worked example. You ask the agent to give pre-orders of a new seasonal flavor three extra days before they count as late. Afterward the suite is green. In the pull request, you read the list of changed files and see that a test file changed too. You ask a fresh conversation with the agent to explain.
It reports that the test “an order shipped one day late is late” used to expect “late.” It now expects “on time.” The agent’s change broke the rule for every order. Instead of fixing its code, it changed the expected answer.
An agent told to “make the tests pass” has three shortcuts. It can change the expected answer, delete the test, or mark the test to be skipped. All three turn the suite green. None of them fixes anything.
Rule of thumb: when a change touches both the app and its tests, review the test changes first. A changed expected answer, a deleted test or a skipped test needs a reason.
crumbs: 6  Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
text:
Your part in testing
You decide what must never break, and you make the agent prove each bug is fixed.
Asking for “tests” with no target gets you tests of whatever was easiest to test. Aim the effort.
A quality engineer does not inspect every dimension of every part. The control plan names the characteristics that are critical to quality, and those get checked every time.
Five habits cover your part.

Ask for tests on what matters. In your app, that means any score or number a manager will act on. It also means anything that changes stored data, and the main path through the app.
Read the test names as a specification. A missing behavior in the list is a missing check.
Confirm the suite ran before you merge. Look at the checks on the pull request, or ask the agent to run the suite and show you the last result.
Read test changes first in any review, as in the example above.
For every bug, ask for a regression test that fails first.

The fifth habit needs a word of explanation. A regression test is a test written for a bug you fixed, so the bug cannot come back unnoticed. Ask for it in a particular order.
Worked example. The owner reports that order 2041 was cancelled after it shipped. You tell the agent, “Before you fix anything, write a test that reproduces this, and show it to me failing.” The agent writes “a shipped order cannot be cancelled.” It runs the test, and the test fails. Then it fixes the code, and the same test passes.
The failing run proves the test can detect the bug. The passing run proves the fix works. A test you never saw fail might not be checking anything.
One more caution. The worst regressions come from changing something that several features share. Suppose the agent changes how dates are handled. That touches the on-time rule, the weekly late-shipments report and the units-sold-per-week calculation. Before it finishes, ask it to list every feature that uses what it changed, and to test each one.
Rule of thumb: no bug is fixed until a test that failed now passes.

section: A second reader: AI code review
text:
A second reader: AI code review
Before you send changes to GitHub, have the agent run a code review that reads them for mistakes.
Tests check what someone thought to check. A code review is a careful reading of a set of changes, looking for mistakes that no test was written for. It looks for a rule that misses a case, a save that can fail without warning, or a change that breaks another feature.
Code review used to need a second programmer, who read each pull request line by line. You could not do that job. An agent can. Claude Code has a code review built in.








What you want
How
When to use it




Review your changes for mistakes
Type /code-review in the message box, or ask “Run a code review of my changes”
Before you send changes to GitHub



With nothing added after it, the review reads the changes you have not yet sent to GitHub. It reports what it found: where each problem is and why it matters. It does not change anything on its own. In the desktop app the findings arrive as a card, with buttons to fix one finding or all of them.
Your part is the same as in session 1. Read the list. Ask the agent to explain any finding you do not understand. Have it fix the ones you agree with. Then run the tests again, because a fix is a change too.
Expect the review to find something. Even a change that passes every test usually has a finding worth fixing.
Accountants work the same way. Many companies require a second person to review a journal entry before it is posted to the books. The person who wrote the entry is the one least likely to see its mistake.
Rule of thumb: review before you send. Fix what you agree with, then test again.

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
text:
Look for yourself
Some evidence you can gather yourself in under a minute, without the agent.

The reload test
An app can keep data in three places, and they are not equally permanent.








Place
How long it lasts
Who can reach it




Page memory
Until the page reloads or the tab closes
This tab only


Browser storage
Until the user clears their browser data
This one browser, on this one device


Database
Until someone deletes it
Every device and user you allow



The rule follows from the table. If data must follow the user to another device, be shared with others or be trusted, it belongs in the database. The copy in the database is the one that counts.
A store knows this as the gap between the system count and the shelf. You do not trust the count on the screen until someone has checked what is actually there.
So here is the simplest test you can run. Enter something, reload the page, and see whether it is still there. If a customer note vanishes on reload, it was only in page memory and was never saved. Then open the app on your phone. If the note is on your computer but not your phone, it was saved in the browser, not the database.


The evidence panels
Session 2 introduced developer tools, the panel built into every browser. In Chrome you open it with the F12 key on Windows, or Command, Option and I on a Mac. Two of its tabs give you evidence.








Tab
The question it answers
Use it when




Console
Did the app’s code hit an error?
A screen is blank, or a button does nothing. Errors appear in red.


Network
What requests went out, and what came back?
Something did not save or load.



Each row in the Network tab is one request, with a number called a status code. You need only three ranges. Codes in the 200s mean the request worked. Codes in the 400s mean the request was wrong or was refused. Codes in the 500s mean the server failed.
When you report a problem to the agent, this is your evidence. “Shipping order 2042 does nothing” is a weak report. Paste the red error from the Console and the status code of the failed request, and the agent starts from facts instead of guesses.


The app’s own record: logs
A log is a running record your app writes as it works: one line for each important action or error, with the time. Developer tools show only what happens in your own browser, right now. A log shows what happened on the server, for every user, after the fact.
Your app writes only what it was told to write. So ask for it: “On the server, write a log line each time an order is shipped or cancelled, and each time a save fails.” A line in the example shop might read “10:14, order 2042 marked shipped.” When the owner says an order changed by itself, the log shows what happened and when.
A bank keeps a record of every transaction for the same reason. When a customer disputes a charge, the record shows what happened.
Later sessions build on this. Session 8 shows where your hosting company keeps the logs, and what a log line must never contain. Session 10 uses a log to check the exact instructions your app sends to an AI model.
Rule of thumb: before you tell the agent something is broken, reload once and copy the error. Then check the log.

title: Testing: How Do You Know It Works? — Vibe Programming, Session 5
section: Technical debt: every shortcut is a loan
text:
Technical debt: every shortcut is a loan
A quick solution now creates extra work later, and the extra work grows the longer you leave it.
Technical debt is the extra work you will have to do later because you chose a quick solution now instead of a better one. Like a loan, it charges interest. Every later change in that part of the app takes longer.
Maintenance managers know this well. Skipping a scheduled maintenance stop to hit this week’s shipment can be the right call. It is a loan against the machine. If nobody writes it down and schedules the make-up work, the machine eventually picks its own time to stop.
Debt comes in two kinds.

Deliberate debt is a shortcut you chose knowingly, with a plan to repay it. “This will not handle ten thousand products, but we need to show it to an investor on Friday.”
Accidental debt is a mess nobody chose. The classic case is the same rule written in three places, which then drift apart.

Agents create accidental debt quickly, because they write quickly. Ask an agent to fix the on-time rule on the order screen, and it may patch that one screen. The weekly late-shipments report keeps its own copy of the rule, with the old mistake.
You can ask about this in plain English: “Find any rule or calculation in this project that is written in more than one place.” Each result is a place where two parts of your app can disagree.
When should you pay debt down? Pay it when it blocks new work or causes errors. Pay it when you are about to change that part of the app anyway. Leave it when the app is still an experiment, or when the cleanup would cost more than it saves. And only clean up where tests exist. Without tests, you cannot tell whether the cleanup changed what the app does.
Rule of thumb: take shortcuts on purpose, and write down each one you take.

title: Databases: Where the Data Lives — Vibe Programming, Session 6
section: The big idea: a prototype forgets, a product remembers
text:
The big idea: a prototype forgets, a product remembers
In session 2 you learned that an app has three places, and that the database is where it keeps what it must remember. In session 5 you ran the reload test and saw the difference. Data in page memory is gone on reload. Data in the database stays.
A database stores an app’s data as tables, and keeps it until someone deletes it. Everything on your screens is a view of what the database holds. The example shop’s sales dashboard is not stored anywhere as a dashboard. It is calculated from rows of orders, every time someone opens it.
Most apps have a database, because most apps must remember things between visits. A few do not. A unit converter or a simple game can forget everything when it closes. Even a simple game may want to remember the high scores, though, and then it needs somewhere to keep them.
Here is the main point of the session: the design of your data is the skeleton of your app. Every screen depends on it, and it is the hardest thing to change later.
You will not write database code. You will decide what the business needs to remember and check that the agent’s design matches the business. You will also catch a question that was answered wrongly.
This session the example shop adds a new part: stock kept at two locations. One is the freezer at the shop’s production kitchen, where the ice cream is made and the cookies are baked. The other is the freezer case and cookie shelf at the shop’s storefront, the shop on campus where customers walk in and buy. Until now the app counted all stock as one number. You will add a new kind of record to your own app as well.

Tables, rows, columns and keys
A database is a set of tables, and keys are how the tables refer to each other.
There are five building blocks.

You already know this structure from a class roster. Each student is one row. Each fact about a student is a column. Your student ID number is a primary key: no two students share it, so it points to exactly one person.

Park moves, you change one row in one table. The Product ID column works the same way, pointing into a table of products.
A table looks like a spreadsheet, and that is a fair first picture. It breaks in two places.

A database enforces rules on every entry. A spreadsheet lets you type “seven” into a number column. A database refuses.
Most of a database’s usefulness comes from the links between tables. A spreadsheet does not have them.

Rule of thumb: record each fact in one place, and point to it from everywhere else.

title: Databases: Where the Data Lives — Vibe Programming, Session 6
text:
Three kinds of database
Databases differ in where they run and who looks after them. The right kind depends on how many people use the app at once.
All three kinds below store tables, rows and keys in the same way. They differ in where the data sits and who keeps it running.









Kind
Examples
Where the data sits
When it fits




Single-file database
SQLite
One file, next to the app
Learning, quick prototypes, and apps used by one person on one device, such as many phone apps


Database server
PostgreSQL, MySQL
A program on a server that answers the app’s requests
Apps with many users at once, when someone on the team can keep it running, backed up and updated


Hosted database
Supabase
A database server that a company runs for you
Small teams that want a real database without running one. Supabase runs PostgreSQL.



A single file is simple, but it is hard to share. Many hosting companies also do not keep the files an app writes, so a single-file database on them can lose its data. A database server handles many users, but someone has to look after it. A hosted database gives you the server without the upkeep, and you pay with a monthly bill and less control.
A company makes the same choice about payroll. A very small business can run payroll from one spreadsheet. A large one may run its own payroll department. Many choose a payroll service that does the work for a fee.
The example shop uses a hosted database, like most apps in this course. Ask the agent which kind your app uses, and where its data is kept.
Rule of thumb: if several people will use your app from different devices, use a database server or a hosted one, not a single file.

title: Databases: Where the Data Lives — Vibe Programming, Session 6
section: From a sentence to a set of tables
text:
From a sentence to a set of tables
The tables are the nouns of the business. For each pair, ask how many of one go with one of the other.
The whole design of tables and their links is called the schema. You can draft one from a sentence.
Start with a description of what the business needs. Underline the nouns. Then take the nouns two at a time and ask how many of one go with one of the other.
Worked example. This session the shop adds stock by location. The description is: “The shop keeps a quantity of each product at each of its locations.”
The nouns are products, locations and quantities. You already have a table of products. Now ask the question about products and locations.

One product can be held at many locations.
One location holds many products.

That is many on both sides. When that happens, you need a third table with one row for each pairing. Call it stock.



Table
Columns




Products
Product ID, name, price


Locations
Location ID, name


Stock
Product ID, location ID, quantity on hand



A row in the stock table says, “product 14, at location 2, quantity 60.” The product ID and location ID are both foreign keys.
Compare that with customers and orders. One customer has many orders, but each order has one customer. That is many on one side only, so no third table is needed. The table on the “many” side, orders, holds the foreign key.
Test yourself on one more pair. In a real shop, one order often holds several products, and each product appears on many orders. That is many on both sides again, so it needs a third table, just like stock: order lines, with one row for each product on each order.
The new tables also connect to what you already have. When the owner ships an order, the quantity on hand at one location should go down. So the shipping step now has to ask which location the package left from. A change to the data often reaches back into a flow you thought was finished.
You can check the agent’s design the same way. Ask it to list every table, its columns and its links, in plain English. Then read the list against the business. Is there a noun the business uses that has no table? Is a fact stored in two places?
Rule of thumb: before the agent builds, write the sentence, underline the nouns, and ask “how many” of each pair.

title: Databases: Where the Data Lives — Vibe Programming, Session 6
section: Rules live in the database, and changes are written down
text:
Rules live in the database, and changes are written down
The database can refuse bad data no matter which screen sent it, and its design should change only through a written, reviewable step.

Rules that hold everywhere
Session 2 taught you that a check in the browser can be skipped. The database is the last line, and it can enforce rules of its own.



Kind of rule
Example in the shop




Type
Quantity must be a whole number


Required
An order must have a customer


Allowed values
Status must be Open, Shipped or Cancelled


Range
Quantity on hand cannot be negative


Link
An order’s customer ID must match a real customer


Unique
No two customers can share an email address



A rule in the database rejects a bad value from any screen, any script and any agent. It cannot be skipped by someone with developer tools.


Why the design is hard to change
Once real rows sit in a table, every screen, calculation and report depends on its shape.
Suppose you stored each customer’s name as one column. Later you want first and last names separately. You must rewrite every existing row and every part of the app that reads it. For a customer entered as “Front Desk, Hotel Aria,” someone has to guess.
A store has the same problem. Changing the floor plan on paper takes an afternoon. Changing it in an open store means moving every shelf and every product. Code can be rewritten quickly. Data has to be moved.


Migrations
A migration is a small file that makes one change to the schema, such as “add a locations table.” Migrations are saved in your project and applied in order.
The alternative is to click around in the database’s own website and add a column by hand. Do not do that, and do not let the agent do it. A migration has three advantages over a click.

It can be reviewed. It appears in a pull request, like any other change from session 3.
It can be repeated. A fresh database can be built by applying the migrations in order.
It is recorded. Your project’s history shows when the design changed, and why.

Rule of thumb: treat a change to the schema as a group 3 action. Have the agent plan it, read the plan, and review the migration before it runs.

title: Databases: Where the Data Lives — Vibe Programming, Session 6
text:
Asking the database a question
Every question to a database is built from the same few blocks, and your job is to predict which rows come back.
A query is a question put to the database. You do not need to write one. You need to tell when the agent’s query answers a different question from the one you asked.
A query is assembled from six blocks.



Block
What it does




Choose the table
Where to look


Filter
Keep only the rows that pass a test


Choose columns
Which facts to return


Sort
Put the rows in order


Limit
Keep only the first few rows after sorting


Join
Pair each row with its matching rows in another table



A shopping list for a busy errand is built the same way. It names the store, the items to get, the details that matter and the order to walk the aisles.
Worked example. Using the tables above, you ask: “Show the order number and quantity for J. Park’s orders that shipped late, newest first.”

Table: orders.
Filter: customer ID is 2, and the shipped date is after the promised date. Order 2038 passes. Order 2040 shipped a day early. Order 2042 has no shipped date, so it is not “after” anything.
Columns: order number and quantity.
Sort: newest first.

The answer is one row: order 2038, quantity 2.
Three things about queries surprise people.
An empty answer is not an error. Ask for R. Alvarez’s late orders and you get no rows. That is a correct answer. It also means a broken filter can look exactly like “nothing to report.”
An empty value is not zero. Order 2042 has no shipped date. It is not late, and it is not on time. A query has to say what to do with it. This is the same edge case you met in session 1.
A join drops rows that have no match. Suppose a report pairs each customer with their orders. A customer who signed up yesterday has none. Unless the query is told to keep that customer, they vanish from the list.

A query that answers the wrong question
Worked example. You ask for “each customer’s most recent order.” The agent sorts all orders by date and keeps the first one. The result is a single row: order 2043 from M. Osei.
The query ran without error. It answered “the most recent order overall.” You asked for one row per customer, which is three rows.
You catch this by predicting before you look, as in session 1. Three customers have orders, so you expect three rows. One row means the question was misread.


Why a screen gets slow
To find J. Park’s orders, the database can read every row in the table. Or it can use an index: a sorted lookup list it keeps on one column, like the index at the back of a book. An index lets it jump straight to the matching rows.
With a few hundred rows you will never notice the difference. If a screen slows down as your data grows, a missing index is the first thing to ask the agent about.
Rule of thumb: before you read a report, predict how many rows it should have.
crumbs: 7  Databases: Where the Data Lives — Vibe Programming, Session 6

title: Databases: Where the Data Lives — Vibe Programming, Session 6
text:
Changing data, and protecting it
An update or a delete uses a filter to pick its rows, and a missing filter changes or erases every row in the table.
A database has four basic operations: create a row, read rows, update rows and delete rows.
The first two are low risk. The last two use the same filter block as a query. “Delete the orders where the status is Cancelled” removes a few rows. Leave off the filter, and the same instruction removes every order you have. There is no trash folder.
Four habits protect your data.
Mark, do not delete. In session 2 you told the agent to store the status Cancelled and never delete the row. Accounting works the same way. A ledger entry is never erased. A correcting entry is posted, with a reason. The shop’s dashboard is calculated from history, so the history has to stay. Marking protects a row from being erased. It does not record who changed a value, or when. That record, called an audit trail, needs the app to know who is acting. Session 7 adds logins.
Make two-table changes all or nothing. Shipping an order changes two tables. The order becomes Shipped, and the stock at one location goes down. If one change saves and the other fails, the data disagrees with itself. A database can group several changes into one transaction, so that they all happen or none do. When one action changes two tables, ask the agent to make it all or nothing. The range rule above also covers two customers buying the last pint at the same moment. The stock cannot go below zero, so the database refuses the second sale.
Back up before a change that alters or removes data. Session 3 taught you that reverting a change restores the files but not the rows. A backup is the only way back.
Do not build against real data. On the first day, your computer copy and your live app can share one database, because there is nothing to lose. Once real people use the app, that changes. Every unfinished feature you try, and every action the agent takes, would act on their data. From then on you build against a separate copy that you can wipe and refill.
That copy is filled with seed data: made-up rows that give the app something to show. Good seed data varies the way real data does. If every product in your seed data sells at the same steady pace, the dashboard will look perfect and tell you nothing.
You can also look at the data directly. The service that runs your database has a screen that shows each table and its rows. Use it to look, the way a store manager walks the aisles to check a count. Do not use it to edit.
Rule of thumb: before any update or delete, ask the agent how many rows it will touch.

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
section: The big idea: so far, your app has trusted everyone
text:
The big idea: so far, your app has trusted everyone
Until now the example shop has had no login. Everyone who opens it sees every customer, every order and every product, and can change them.
That was fine for a class project with made-up data. This session the shop gets two kinds of user. Staff run the shop. Customers can sign in to their own online portal, see what is in stock, place an order and follow their own orders. Products now also record the shop’s cost, what it paid for each item. A customer must not see the shop’s costs, its sales dashboard or another customer’s orders. Your own app needs the same kind of thinking: who uses it, and what each kind of user may see.
In session 2 you learned the trust line. The user controls the browser, so hiding something on a screen protects nothing. This session applies that idea to people.
Here is the main point of the session: signing in proves who someone is. It does not decide what they may do. That second decision must be enforced where the data lives.

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
section: Two questions: who are you, and what may you do?
text:
Two questions: who are you, and what may you do?
Security in an app comes down to two separate questions, and confusing them is the most common mistake.








Question
Name
Answered




Who is this?
Authentication
Once, at sign-in


May this person do this, to this record?
Authorization
On every request



An office building handles visitors the same way. At the front desk, a guard checks your identification once and gives you a badge. That is authentication. After that, every door reads the badge and decides whether it opens for you. That is authorization. A contractor’s badge is real, and it still does not open the finance office.
The common mistake is to treat authorization as a screen problem. The agent hides the Edit button from customers and reports that customers cannot edit. But the button is in the browser, and so is the request it would have sent. Anyone can send that request by hand.
Worked example. The shop has a page for editing products and prices. Customers never see a link to it. A curious customer types the page’s address directly, and the page loads, because the only protection was the missing link.
Now add a rule in the database that lets only staff change the products table. The page may still load. But every attempt to save fails. That is the result you want. The screen is a courtesy. The rule is the protection.
Rule of thumb: when the agent says a user “cannot” do something, ask what stops them. If the answer is a hidden button, nothing stops them.
crumbs: 8  Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
section: Signing in: let a service do it
text:
Signing in: let a service do it
Handling passwords safely is hard, and a sign-in service already does it. Do not build your own.
Sign-in looks simple. Underneath, someone must store passwords so that a thief who copies the database cannot read them. Someone must handle forgotten passwords, confirm email addresses and remember who is signed in. Each of these has been done wrong by serious companies.
The service that runs your database also offers sign-in. It can check an email and password. It can also let people sign in through another service they already trust, such as “Sign in with Google.” In that case the other service vouches for who the user is.
A company makes the same choice about its building. It does not design its own lock and badge system. It buys one from a firm that does nothing else, and spends its own effort deciding who gets which badge.

What happens at sign-in

The user types an email and a password.
The sign-in service checks them.
If they are correct, it gives the browser a token: a long, signed string that says who the user is.
The browser sends that token with every later request.
The server and the database read the token to learn who is asking.

The token is your visitor badge. Three facts about it matter.

It cannot be edited. The service signs it, so a changed token is rejected.
It expires. A token lasts a short time and is renewed in the background while you stay signed in.
Whoever holds it is you. Anyone who copies your token can act as you until it expires.

That last fact gives you a rule. Never paste a token into a chat, an email, a support ticket or a prompt to an AI.
Rule of thumb: ask the agent to use the sign-in service that comes with your stack. If it starts writing its own password handling, stop it.
crumbs: 8  Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
section: Access rules live in the database
text:
Access rules live in the database
An access rule belongs on the table it protects, so it holds no matter which screen or request asks.
Start by writing your rules in plain English, one line per role and table. This is a business decision, and it is yours to make.








Table
Staff may
A customer may




Products
Read and change everything
Read the name and price, but not the cost


Stock
Read and change everything
Read what is available, and where


Orders
Read everything
Create an order, and read only their own


Customers
Read everything
Read and change only their own details



The database can enforce rules like these row by row. A rule of this kind is called a policy. It is attached to a table, and it says which rows a request may touch, based on who is asking.
The clearest way to picture a policy is as a filter the database adds silently to every query. Take the rule “a customer may read only their own orders.” When J. Park asks for all orders, the database behaves as if the request were “all orders where the customer is J. Park.” Only J. Park’s rows come back, whatever the browser requested.
A policy chooses rows, not columns. It cannot hide one column, such as the cost, while showing the rest of the row. Asked to hide the cost, the agent will probably hide it on the screen. That is the mistake this reading warns against. The cost still arrives in the browser, where developer tools can show it. Hiding a column needs a different tool, such as keeping costs in a separate staff-only table. Ask the agent which tool it used.
A bank works this way. One system holds millions of accounts. Each customer can see and move money only in their own. That rule is enforced by the bank’s system on every transaction. It is not a sign on the door.
In the stack this course uses, this matters even more than usual. Session 2 mentioned that the browser can send requests straight to the database. When it does, there is no server in between to check anything. The database’s own rules are the only protection.

Two situations to recognize on sight








Situation
What you see
What it means




Rules are switched off for a table
The app works perfectly
Anyone who has opened your app can read and change every row, signed in or not


Rules are switched on, but no policy has been written
A list that should have rows is empty
Nobody is allowed to read anything yet



The first is dangerous precisely because nothing looks wrong. The second explains a common puzzle. When the rules block a read, the database does not report an error. It returns an empty list. To the app, “you may not see these rows” and “there are no rows” look the same. You met that in session 6.
Worked example. Your app shows each customer only their own orders, because the page asks the database for “orders where the customer is me.” The rules on the orders table are switched off. A customer opens developer tools, removes that filter from the request and downloads every customer’s orders.
The page’s filter was a convenience. A policy on the table would have enforced the restriction.
Rule of thumb: for every table, you should be able to say who may read it and who may change it. If you cannot, nobody has decided.
crumbs: 8  Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
text:
Test it with two accounts
You find out whether access is enforced by signing in as someone who should be refused and trying anyway.
Reading the rules is not enough. Neither is the agent’s report. This is session 1’s third question again: how will you know it worked?
A good auditor does not read the door policy and go home. The auditor walks the building and tries the handles.
The two-account test takes five minutes.

Create two customer accounts, A and B.
Sign in as A and place an order.
Sign in as B. Try to see A’s order, change it and delete it.
Try three ways. Use the screens. Type the address of A’s order into the address bar. Ask the agent to send the request directly while signed in as B.
Repeat as a customer trying to reach a staff page, and as a customer trying to make themselves staff.
Each time, look at what came back in developer tools, not only at the screen. A hidden column may still have arrived.

If any attempt succeeds, you have found a hole. Have the agent fix it with a policy on the table, then run the test again.
Then make it permanent. In session 5 you learned to ask for tests on what matters. A permission test signs in as one user and confirms that they cannot read or change another user’s data. Ask the agent to write the two-account test as permission tests, so it runs on every pull request.
One detail makes a permission test worthless if it is wrong. The test must sign in as an ordinary user. A test that connects with the secret key, covered next, skips every rule and proves nothing.
Rule of thumb: an access rule is not finished until you have watched it refuse someone.
crumbs: 8  Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
section: Keys: public by design, or secret
text:
Keys: public by design, or secret
Some keys are meant to be seen by everyone, and others must never leave your server. The difference decides where each may live.
Session 2 taught you that a secret key stays on the server. Now there are two kinds of key to tell apart.








Kind of key
What it can do
Where it may live




Public by design
Identifies your app to the database. It can do only what your policies allow.
In the browser. Every visitor receives it.


Secret
Skips every policy, or spends your money at a paid service
On the server only



The public key is not a mistake or a leak. It is safe because your policies stand behind it. This is why the first situation in the last section is so dangerous. With the rules switched off, the public key opens everything.
Think of a building again. The street address is public. The master key is not. Knowing the address lets you walk up to the door, where the badge reader decides. The master key opens every door and ignores the badge readers.

When a secret leaks
Secrets leak in ordinary ways. Someone pushes the secrets file to GitHub. Someone pastes a key into a chat to ask for help. The agent places a key in a file that is sent to the browser.
Deleting the key from the file is not enough. Session 3 taught you that Git keeps every earlier version, so the key is still in the history. It may already have been copied.
The fix is to rotate the key. You create a new key at the service that issued it, and you cancel the old one. This is what a building does when a master key goes missing. It changes the locks.
When a key does not work, ask the agent to check its shape, not to show it. The agent can report how long the key is and whether it starts with the expected letters. Anything printed on the screen stays in the conversation.
Rule of thumb: if a secret has been anywhere it should not be, rotate it. Do not try to work out whether anyone saw it.
crumbs: 8  Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
text:
Data that must not travel
Sending data to another service copies it to that company’s computers, and some data has rules about where it may go.
Your app will hold data that is not yours to share.

Personal data: names, email addresses, phone numbers and anything else that identifies a person.
Business data from others: a supplier’s price list, a customer’s order history, anything received under a contract or a confidentiality agreement.
Credentials: passwords and keys.

The rule that builders most often miss is this: sending data somewhere is copying it there. That includes more places than people expect.







Where data goes
Example




A prompt to an AI model
“Summarize these customer complaints,” with names attached


A log
A line that records the full contents of a sign-up form


An AI coding agent
Letting the agent read a file of real customer records


An outside service
Sending order details to an email or analytics service



Professionals already live by this. An accountant does not forward one client’s tax return to another firm because it was convenient. Once you send it, a copy sits on someone else’s system, and you cannot take it back.
Before data goes anywhere, ask three questions. Does the person or company it belongs to know? Does the contract allow it? Does it need to go at all?
Five habits follow.

Collect only what the feature needs.
Keep personal data in the database, behind policies, and nowhere else.
Have logs record what happened and an ID, never a person’s details. “Customer 42: order failed” is enough.
Remove names before sending text to an AI model, when the task does not need them.
Use made-up data while you build. Do not put real customer or supplier data into any AI tool until you have checked the contract and the tool’s terms.

The fifth habit applies to your first job. If your employer hands you real customer data, the question of which AI tools may see it is not yours to answer alone.
Rule of thumb: before you paste anything into an AI tool, ask whose data it is.
crumbs: 8  Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
section: Run a security review now and then
text:
Run a security review now and then
An AI security review reads your changes for weaknesses you did not think to test.
The two-account test checks the rules you thought of. A security review looks for the ones you missed. Examples are a table with no policy, a secret key in browser code, or a form that lets a user slip in commands.
Claude Code has one built in.








What you want
How
When to use it




Check your changes for security weaknesses
Type /security-review in the message box
Before a change to sign-in, access rules, keys or personal data goes live, and every few weeks



The review reports what it found and why each finding matters. Read the findings with the same care as session 5’s code review. Ask the agent to explain any you do not understand, then have it fix the ones that apply. Then run the two-account test again, because a fix is a change too.
Companies hire outside testers once or twice a year for the same reason. The people who built the locks are the ones least likely to spot the open window.
A review is a second line, not the first. It does not replace the two-account test or your own decisions about who may see what.
Rule of thumb: review security before a risky change goes live, and on a schedule even when nothing seems wrong.

title: Logins and Security: Who May Do What — Vibe Programming, Session 7
text:
Key terms







Term
Plain-English meaning




Authentication
Proving who a user is


Authorization
Deciding what a user may do, to which records


Token
A long, signed string the browser receives at sign-in and sends with every request to prove who is asking


Role
A kind of user, such as staff or customer, with its own set of permissions


Cost
What the shop paid for a product, as opposed to the price it charges


Policy
A rule attached to a table that says which rows a request may touch, based on who is asking


Two-account test
Signing in as one user and trying to reach another user’s data


Permission test
An automated test that confirms one user cannot read or change another user’s data


Public key
A key every visitor receives, which can do only what your policies allow


Secret key
A key that skips every policy or spends your money, and so stays on the server


Rotate
To replace a leaked key with a new one and cancel the old one


Personal data
Anything that identifies a person, such as a name, email address or phone number


Security review
An AI reading of your changes that looks for security weaknesses

text:
Name the three environments your app runs in, and say what defines an environment.
Find out which database each environment uses, and explain why that matters.
Explain the difference between publishing a change and releasing it to users.
Choose between a staging environment and a feature flag for a risky change.
Roll back a bad publish, say what a rollback cannot undo, and find out what went wrong from the logs.

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
section: The big idea: more than one copy, and a way back
text:
The big idea: more than one copy, and a way back
You have been publishing since the intro session. In session 3 you learned the gate: a pull request, a preview and a merge. After the merge, your hosting company publishes the change, and users have it.
Until now that has been safe, because nobody depended on your app. After session 7 it has staff, customers and orders. A bad change now reaches real people and real data.
Publishing a new version of an app is called a deployment. People say “deploy” as a verb.
Here is the main point of the session: your app runs as more than one copy. You try a change on a copy that cannot hurt anyone. You also keep a fast way back for when a bad change gets through.
crumbs: 9  Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
section: Environments: three copies of your app
text:
Environments: three copies of your app
An environment is one running copy of your app, defined by which code it runs, where it runs and which settings it reads.
You already have three. You met two of them in session 2 and the third in session 3.









Environment
Which code
Where it runs
Who sees it




Your computer
Whatever you are working on, including changes you have not saved as a commit
Your own computer, at an address starting with localhost
Only you


Preview
The latest commit on one branch or pull request
The hosting company’s computers, at its own address
Anyone you send the address to


Production
main
The hosting company’s computers, at your app’s real address
Your users



Production is the proper name for what earlier sessions called the live app.
A theater works the same way. Actors rehearse in a practice room, hold a dress rehearsal on the real stage, and then perform for a paying audience. Nobody rehearses in front of the audience.
One difference between the copies will surprise you. The computer copy is put together a page at a time, as you open each page, and it tolerates some mistakes. For a preview or for production, the hosting company makes a build: the whole app assembled at once, the way it will actually run. Some mistakes appear only in the build. An app can work on your computer and still fail to publish.
That is why the build is one of the checks on a pull request, as you saw in session 5.
Rule of thumb: “it works on my computer” is a statement about one environment. Check the preview before you merge.
crumbs: 9  Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
text:
The settings decide the database
An environment uses whichever database its settings name, so a copy of the app is not automatically a copy of the data.
The settings an environment reads are a short list of names and values kept outside the code. Session 2 called the computer’s version the secrets file. The list includes the address of the database and the keys to reach it.
This leads to a fact that is easy to miss. The code and the database are separate choices. If your computer’s settings hold the production database’s address and keys, your computer is working on production data.
It is like a store’s cash register in training mode. The screens look identical to the real ones. Whether a sale you ring up is practice or real depends on which mode the register is in.
Worked example. You set up your project in the intro session with one database. Its address and keys went into your computer’s settings and into the hosting company’s settings for previews and production. All three environments share one database.
Now trace what happens.

A test order you place on your computer appears in front of real customers.
A reviewer who clicks around a preview of an unfinished feature changes real stock quantities.
The made-up seed data from session 6, loaded on your computer, lands in the live tables.

Your computer often holds the secret key too. Session 7 taught you that the secret key skips every policy. A mistake there reaches every user’s data.
Session 6 gave the rule. Once real people use your app, stop building against its database. Give the computer and the previews a database of their own.








Option
What it is
Good for




One database for everything
Computer, previews and production share one
Only until the first real user signs up


A second database
A separate one with the same tables, filled with seed data
Your computer and your previews


A database on your computer
A copy that runs on your own computer
Your computer and your tests. Previews cannot reach it.



The migrations from session 6 pay off here. Applying the same migrations to the second database gives it the same tables as production.
You can check your own setup in one request: “Which database does each of my environments use? Tell me the names only. Do not print any key.”
Rule of thumb: before you load test data or try an unfinished feature, know which database you are pointed at.
crumbs: 9  Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
section: Staging: a rehearsal that matches the real thing
text:
Staging: a rehearsal that matches the real thing
Staging is a copy of your app that closely matches production, where you try a change before any user sees it.
A staging environment has its own data and is not open to users. It is useful in proportion to how closely it matches production. It should be built the same way, hold the same settings with staging values, and have the same tables. Its database is separate.
Every difference from production is a place where “it worked on staging” may not hold in production. So keep the differences few, and write them down. Two differences are always needed.

Outgoing messages. A staging app must not email real customers. It sends only to your own team.
Money. Anything that charges a card runs in the payment service’s test mode.

A new restaurant rehearses this way with a soft opening. It serves a full evening of meals to friends and family before the public opening. The rehearsal is worth something only if the kitchen is set up the way it will be on opening night.
The simplest staging setup costs nothing extra. Point your previews at the second database from the last section. Then every pull request’s preview is a staging site for that one change.
What goes in the staging database? Seed data, or your own team’s accounts. Do not copy real customers’ personal data into staging. Session 7’s rule still applies: copying data somewhere is sending it there.
Rule of thumb: a staging environment with old tables or missing settings tells you little. Keep it matched, or do not trust it.
crumbs: 9  Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
text:
Publishing is not releasing
A change can be published to production and still be switched off, so that you choose who sees it and when.
So far, “published” and “available to users” have been the same moment. They do not have to be.
A feature flag is a setting the app checks before it shows new behavior. The new code is published to production for everyone. The flag decides, for each user, whether they get it. Turning the flag on for someone is called a release. It needs no new deployment. Turning it off stops the new behavior on the next request.
The example shop does this with a new seasonal flavor. Ice cream keeps for months frozen, so the pints can sit in the freezer for weeks before the flavor appears in the online catalog. Stocking it and listing it are separate decisions. The shop may show it to its regular customers first.
A flag can be kept in two ways.







Where the flag is kept
What it allows




In an environment’s settings
On or off for everyone in that environment, such as on in previews and off in production


In a table in your database
On for you, then for twenty customers, then for everyone, by editing a row



Two cautions come with flags. First, check the flag on the server as well as on the screen. A hidden button over a working request can still be used, as you learned in sessions 2 and 7. Second, remove the flag once the feature is on for everyone. Forgotten flags are a kind of technical debt.

Staging or a flag?
They answer different questions.




Staging
Feature flag




Where the new code runs
A separate copy of the app
Production


Whose data it touches
Test data
Real users’ data


Who sees it
Your team
The users the flag is on for


How you undo it
Nothing reached production
Turn the flag off



Ask two questions about the change.

Does it take effect for everyone the moment it is published? A migration does. So does a changed setting. A flag cannot hide these, so try them on staging first.
If the first people who get it hit the worst case, whose data is harmed, and can it be undone? If the harm is limited to your own team’s data, a flag is enough. Some changes could do something permanent to someone outside your team, such as emailing customers. Try those on staging first, then release them behind a flag.

Worked example. The shop wants a reorder suggestion on the stock screen, using each product’s reorder point. It needs a new column in the products table.

Computer. The agent builds it on a branch, against your computer’s database, with the feature behind a flag.
Preview on staging data. The migration is applied to the second database. You click through the preview. This is the first time the migration has run on tables shaped like production’s.
Production, flag off. You apply the migration to production and merge. The code is published. Customers and staff see no change.
Release. You turn the flag on for your own staff account, then for all staff.
Clean up. A small pull request removes the flag.

Rule of thumb: staging protects other people’s data. A flag controls who sees a change. Many teams use both.
crumbs: 9  Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
text:
Rolling back a bad publish
When production is broken, go back to the last good version first, and find the cause afterward.
Fixing a problem while users are hitting it is slow and error-prone. Returning to the last good version takes seconds and lets you fix the cause calmly.
A production line has a cord any operator can pull to stop the line. Nobody is expected to diagnose the defect while bad units keep coming off the end. You stop first.
You have two ways back.








Way back
What it does
When to use it




Rollback at the hosting company
Points your app’s address back at an earlier published version, in seconds. Your project’s files do not change.
First, when production is broken


Revert (session 3)
Makes a new commit that undoes the bad one. Merging it publishes the undo.
Afterward, to make the undo permanent in your project



One detail catches people. After a rollback, the hosting company may stop publishing new merges automatically until you tell it to resume. Your fix can be merged and still not be live. Check after any rollback.

What a rollback cannot undo
Session 3 gave the limit, and it applies here in full. Every published version shares one production database. A rollback changes which code runs. It does not touch the rows.
Suppose a bad publish ran for ten minutes and marked forty orders as shipped. After the rollback, the old code runs against forty wrong rows.
The worst case is a migration that removes something. If the bad publish deleted a column, the old code now runs against a table it does not fit.
So migrations should add before they remove. Adding a column is safe, because old code ignores a column it does not use. Removing one deserves a backup first, and a run on staging.


Repairing the data afterward
The rollback stops the damage. Repairing the rows is a second, slower job.

Find the rows. Ask the agent which rows the bad version changed, using the time window and the logs covered below.
Plan the repair. In plan mode, have the agent propose how to put each row back. Read the plan, and ask how many rows it will touch, as in session 6.
Restore if you must. If the damage is too wide to repair row by row, restore the database from a backup taken before the bad publish. Changes made since that backup are lost, so this is the last resort.

A restore needs a backup to exist. Database plans differ in whether they keep backups and how far back they go. Find out what yours keeps now, before you need it.
Rule of thumb: practice a rollback once on a harmless change, and check what backups you have. The first time you need either should not be the first time you look.
crumbs: 9  Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
text:
See what is happening: logs
You cannot fix what you cannot see, and most users who hit an error leave without telling you.
A log is a line of text the app writes when something happens. An error report is a record of a failure with its details, collected automatically.
Each of the three places from session 2 keeps its own record.








Where it ran
Where to look
What you find




Browser
The Console and Network tabs from session 5
Errors on that one device


Server
The hosting company’s logs
Errors and messages from your server code


Database
The database service’s logs
Refused requests and failed sign-ins



The browser’s record is only on the device in front of you. To see what real users hit, an app can add an error reporting service. It collects every failure from every user, groups them and can email you.
A package leaves a record the same way. Each handoff is scanned. When a package goes missing, nobody guesses. They read the scan history and find the last place it was seen.
A useful log line says what happened, where, and an ID you can trace: “Ship order 2042, staff 7, refused: order is cancelled.” It must not hold personal data, passwords or tokens. Session 7’s rule applies, because logs are stored by your hosting company and can be read by anyone on the project.
One practical warning. On free plans, hosting companies keep server logs for only a short time. Look soon after a problem.
Rule of thumb: when a user reports a problem, get the time it happened. Then read the logs before you ask the agent to guess.

title: Deployment: Publishing, and Undoing a Bad Publish — Vibe Programming, Session 8
text:
Key terms







Term
Plain-English meaning




Deployment
Publishing a new version of an app


Environment
One running copy of the app: which code, where it runs and which settings it reads


Preview
A copy of the app built from one branch or pull request, at its own address


Production
The copy at your app’s real address, which your users use


Build
The whole app assembled at once, the way it will actually run


Staging
An environment kept as close to production as possible, with its own data, for trying a change


Feature flag
A setting the app checks to decide which users get new behavior


Release
Turning a published feature on for some or all users


Rollback
Pointing the app’s address back at an earlier published version


Log
A line of text the app writes when something happens


Error report
A record of a failure with its details, collected automatically

Adapted and simplified from parts of three of Scott Murff’s chapters, Data and APIs, Anatomy of an Application and Directing the Agent, in his textbook Intro to Product Management. The ideas are his. The wording and the business examples were written for these readings.

title: Connections: APIs and MCP — Vibe Programming, Session 9
text:
Explain what an API is, and give examples of jobs your app could hand to an outside service.
Name the questions to ask before you connect your app to a service.
Say where the secret key travels when your app calls a service, and why the browser never holds it.
Decide what the user should see when a connection fails, and test it.

title: Connections: APIs and MCP — Vibe Programming, Session 9
section: The big idea: your app does not have to do everything itself
text:
The big idea: your app does not have to do everything itself
So far your app has talked only to its own server and its own database. Real business software rarely works alone. It sends email through one company, takes card payments through another, and gets tracking numbers from a delivery company.
Session 2 defined an API as the list of requests a system agrees to answer. When your app uses another company’s API, it can do things you could never build yourself in a semester.
This session the example shop makes its first outside connection. It will email a shipping notice to a customer when an order ships. Your own app will make one outside connection of its own.
There is a second subject. Your agent can also connect to your other tools while it builds, such as GitHub or a spreadsheet. A standard called MCP makes that possible.
Here is the main point of the session: an outside connection lets your app or your agent do much more, but it reaches beyond your control. Choose each one on purpose, and decide what happens when it fails.
crumbs: 10  Connections: APIs and MCP — Vibe Programming, Session 9

title: Connections: APIs and MCP — Vibe Programming, Session 9
section: What an API lets your app do
text:
What an API lets your app do
An API lets your app hand a job to another company’s service, without knowing how that service works inside.
The company that offers an API publishes its documentation. It lists each request the service accepts, what the request must include and what comes back. Your app never sees the company’s code or computers. As long as the documented requests keep working, your app keeps working. So the documentation works as a contract between the two sides.
You do not need to read the documentation yourself. The agent reads it. Your job is to decide which jobs are worth handing out.
Here are jobs that apps commonly hand to an outside service.









Job
What the service does
In the example shop
In other apps




Send email
Delivers messages so they do not land in spam
A shipping notice to the customer
A reminder to club members before an event


Take payments
Handles card numbers safely, so your app never stores them
Online orders paid by card
Membership dues or ticket sales


Send text messages
Delivers a text to a phone number
“Your order is ready for pickup at the storefront”
A shift reminder for staff


Check addresses and maps
Confirms an address exists, or finds distances
Catching a mistyped shipping address before the box goes out
Finding the nearest volunteer site


Track shipments
Reports where a package is
A tracking link in the shipping notice
Status updates on a supplier’s delivery


Answer with AI
Sends text to an AI model and returns its reply
Session 10
Session 10



Each of these is a business of its own. Sending email reliably takes years of work with the big email providers. Holding card numbers safely takes audits and legal agreements. Using a service is a decision to rent that work instead of doing it.
A shop makes the same choice about delivery. It does not buy trucks and hire drivers. It opens an account with a delivery company, and the delivery company does the driving.
Worked example. Look at the shop’s orders. When an order ships, the owner currently has to email the customer by hand, and some customers are never told. An email service can send the notice the moment the owner clicks Mark shipped. That saves the owner time, and customers stop calling to ask where their ice cream is.
Now look at your own app. Which job does a person do by hand that an outside service could do? That is a candidate for your connection this session.
Rule of thumb: connect to a service when the job is someone else’s specialty and doing it by hand is costing you time or customers.

title: Connections: APIs and MCP — Vibe Programming, Session 9
text:
Before you connect: five questions
A service is a supplier, so check it the way you would check a supplier before you sign.
Ask the agent to answer these five questions for any service you are considering. It can read the documentation and the pricing page for you. Then check its answers on the company’s own website.

What does it cost? Many services have a free tier, a set amount of use each month at no charge. Find out what happens when you pass it.
What account and key do I need? Most services give your account an API key, the secret from session 2 that says whose account is calling. Your account gets the bill.
What are the limits? A rate limit is a cap on how many requests you may send in a period, such as 100 emails a day.
What data will I send it? Session 7’s rule applies. Personal data that leaves your database is in the other company’s hands.
What if it goes down, or I want to leave? Your feature stops working when the service does. And the more your app depends on one service, the harder it is to switch later.

A purchasing team asks the same questions about a new supplier: price, terms, capacity, what you must share with them and how hard they are to replace.
Worked example. You ask the agent to compare two email services for the shop’s shipping notices. It reports that both are free for the shop’s few dozen emails a day. One needs the shop to prove it owns its sending address. Both need a key. The notice holds a customer’s name, email address and order. That is personal data, but it is exactly what an email service must have to do the job. You choose one and note the daily limit in your instruction file.
Rule of thumb: before the agent connects a service, ask it to answer the five questions in plain English.

title: Connections: APIs and MCP — Vibe Programming, Session 9
section: How a call works: the key stays on your server
text:
How a call works: the key stays on your server
Any request that carries a secret key goes from your server, never from the browser.
Session 2 gave the rule about secret keys. If a key reaches the browser, any user can read it with developer tools and use your account. For an email service, that means sending mail in your name, on your bill. So the browser never talks to the email service. It asks your server, and your server makes the call.
A hotel front desk works the same way. A guest asks the desk to book a car to the airport. The desk books it on the hotel’s own account, and the guest never sees the account number.
Worked example. The owner clicks “Send shipping notice” on order 2042.

The browser asks your server: “Send the notice for order 2042.”
Your server checks the request. Is this user staff? Does order 2042 exist? Has the notice already been sent?
Your server sends a request to the email service, with your key and the order details.
The email service sends the message and replies to your server.
Your server records in the database that the notice was sent, and when.
Your server tells the browser, which shows “Notice sent to J. Park at 2:14 p.m.”

The secret key appears in exactly one message: the one between your server and the email service.
You can see this for yourself. Ask the agent, “Show me the request you send to the email service and the reply you get, with the key hidden.” The request is usually written in a plain-text format called JSON: labels and values inside curly braces, such as { "order_number": 2042, "customer": "J. Park" }. You can read it without training.
Earlier sessions apply here too.

Session 1. Sending an email is a group 3 action. It cannot be recalled. A notice sent to the wrong customer is in their inbox, along with someone else’s order.
Session 4. The Send button changes data. It must show that it is working and refuse a second click.
Session 8. Your computer and your previews must not email real customers. In those environments, the app sends only to your own address.

Rule of thumb: for any outside connection, be able to say which message carries the key, and confirm that the browser is not in it.

title: Connections: APIs and MCP — Vibe Programming, Session 9
text:
When a connection fails
A request crosses the internet to a computer you do not control, so a good app expects failure and tells the user what happened.
Every reply from a service carries a status code, the number you met in session 5. The agent reads the code. Your job is to decide what the user sees for each kind of failure.







What went wrong
What the user should see




Something the user entered was missing or wrong
What to fix


The app’s key is wrong or expired
“Something went wrong on our end,” and a message to the owner


The app sent too many requests too fast, past the rate limit
“Busy. Try again in a moment.”


The service is down
“Something went wrong on our end. Try again later.”


No reply at all, before a time limit runs out
“We are not sure this went through. Please check before trying again.”



That time limit is called a timeout. A spinner that never stops is usually a request that is still waiting for one.
Shipping has the same list under other names. A delivery can be refused or sent to an address that does not exist. It can be held because the carrier is overloaded, or lost with no scan at all. A carrier reports each one differently, because each needs a different response.

What agents leave out
An agent builds the happy path first, as you learned in session 4. For a connection, that means it often makes the call and assumes it worked. Then a failed send looks exactly like a successful one. The owner sees “Sent,” and the customer never gets the notice.
Worked example. You test the Send button by turning off your Wi-Fi and clicking it. The screen says “Notice sent to J. Park.” Nothing was sent. The app never checked the reply.
You ask the agent to handle every case in the table. For each one, the app should show a clear message and log the attempt, as in sessions 5 and 8. When the service clearly refused, the order stays marked as not sent.
A timeout is different. The email service may have sent the message before its reply was lost. Marking it “not sent” invites a second click, and the customer gets the notice twice. Session 6 taught you that an empty value is not zero. In the same way, no reply is not a failure. Mark the notice “send status unknown,” and have someone check before resending.
Rule of thumb: for every connection, ask what the user sees when it fails. If the answer is “nothing,” or “the same as success,” it is not finished.
